A Present for Oronstadt. þÿ Through the favour of Messrs. Finch and Kelly, we have had j the satisfaction of viewing one of those considerable presents which we intend next year to j shower into Cronstadt and Helsingfors in such numbers as will prove the sincerity of our into- | rest in those strongholds, if, indeed it shall not overwhelm them. The present we refer to is an immense bomb-shell of the hugest and most extraordinary proportions þÿ one of a number which the Lowmoor Iron Company is under contract with the Government to supply, and which the company is now rapidly casting and completing. This shell is nine feet five inches in circumference, and 36 inches in diameter. The aperture by which it is charged and the fuse inserted arc 2® inches in diameter, and the shell itself inches thick throughout, and at the aperture 3J inches. The weigLt of the shell is 1 ton 6 cwt. lqr. 7lb. With such dimensions and such weight it is easy to understand that when propelled by adequate projectile force no granite can withstand those monster shells ; and Cronstadt must crumble before the repeated and sustained operation of such a bombardment. This immense shell has been sent to the þÿcompany s Liverpool agents for transmission to the Duke of þÿDevonshire castle, s in Listnorc, Ireland, the company having, at the

þÿDuke s request, presented him with one uncharged. Of course such a weight of metal will require considerable leverage to place it within the chamber of a mortar, and this cannot be done without a resort to machinery, to facilitate which we should state that the mouth of the shell is surrounded at a convenient distance by four lugs, made of wrought-iron and cast into the shell, which, by these means, is placed within the mortar. The cost of each shell unfilled will be £20 to £2), and, however expensive, we could not send his Czarship an uglier present or one more unwelcome. The mortars for the discharge of these monster shells are in course of manufacture at the works of Mr. C. Mare, Blackwall They are of wrought-iron, and will weigh about 35 tons each. þÿ Liverpool Post. The number of men and boys now employed at Woolwich Arsenal exceeds 9,000.
THE CRIMEA. A short letter from a correspondent in the camp, dated Dec. 1 1 , gives some further news of the small affair between the French and Russians

3 1 A'UB, at Baga, already reported. The correspondent says : þÿ As the French have retired in the presence of winter, the enemy have thrown forward their advanced posts at Koluluz and Markul to the north-east, and from Aitodor and Ozenbash to the north of Baidar. Sunday morning was dark and drizzly, and the previous night had been wet and stormy. The Russians, with their usual feline aptitude for surprises, crept round the little village of Baga in the dark, and just at the dawn rushed in upon the small party of French which occupied it. For a time the surprise was complete ; but our gallant allies soon got together, and at the point of the bayonet, after a smart fusillade, drove out the enemy, who had many horsemen with them. In the pursuit of the Cossacks our allies managed to capture some forty horses. In this affair the French had one officer mortally wounded, seven men killed, and thirteen wounded; and the Russians are said to have left seventy dead on the ground, and twenty men prisoners in the hands of the þÿFrench.

A Council ok War. þÿ A council of war will shortly be held at Paris, at which the Duke of Cambridge, attended by Sir R. Airey, will be present. Sir E. Lyons, too, will join in the conference, and may be daily expected at Marseilles The object of this meeting will be to weigh thoroughly the several plans for the next campaign, and, when a decision is formed, to carry out combined operations with energy and completeness. Marshal Pelissier has been foremost in requesting that this council should be held It ! will be remembered that during the months of September and October the French crossed the Valley of Baidar, seized the heights to the north, pushed forward a division to the head-waters of the Belbek, and threatened the passes of Aitodor and Albat. At that time an opinion was expressed that the Russian plateau, steep as a wall towards the south, and to be gained only by narrow passes, was a position not to be attacked. What plan of campaign is resolved on will, of course, be a secret till the hour for its execution arrives.

The Port of Spain Gazette, of the 12th inst., which has been kindly lent us by a mercantile friend in town, makes the following startling announcement of large forgeries perpetrated at the Colonial Bank : þÿ þÿ Our community, and especially the mercan- j tile portion of it, have been for the last two days in a state of painful excitement, deluged with rumours and reports of forgeries having been successfully perpetrated on the Bank to an indefinite, if not alarming extent. A committee of investigation, comprising one of our highest legal authorities, have been engaged in examining into the affair As their labours are unfinished, we can as yet give no account of the results, and as we are not desirous of filling our pages with the surmises and suspicions that have been so prolifically produced, we shall simply give a statement of those facts which are both undisputed, and not likely, by being published, to interfere with the pursuit of the investigation. Forged cheques of Messrs. Ambard, P. B. Andre, Laughlin, and Wainwright, to the amount of £2,206 were paid by the Bank on the 8th and 25th of October. This, we believe we may confidently state, is the extent of the fraud þÿ under $10,000. The most extraordinary part of the business is, that these forged cheques, after being crossed by the Cashier, and entered by the Clerk, have, together with others of the same initial letters, and therefore from the same pigeon-holes, been surreptitiously extracted, and cannot be recovered ; so that the forgeries them-

selves are not in hand. There is one exception to this, however. About the same time a cheque was found in Brunswick Square, purporting to be drawn by the Hon. K. S Darling, whose signature upon it is so cleverly imitated as to puzzle those most intimate with his handwriting. Tliis cheque was taken to that þÿgentleman store, s and it was there ascertained that it had not been drawn by Mr. Darling. It appears that no suspicion was awakened, that the man was rewarded for his honesty, and there the matter rested, till the recent discovery, when it is at once supposed that this cheque and those that have been paid had a common origin. Information of the whole matter has been transmitted to the principal establishment at Barbados, and we believe the in- \ quiry must rest till some one arrives from I thence þÿ

Tian«|»»Kition of Figures. The Figure Nine. þÿ We take the following from the Boston Courier. It is an arithmetical curiosity, interesting for the general reader and important to accounttints: þÿ The numeral nine has a certain pecu. liar property, a knowledge of which will he of importance to accountants and cash-keepers. It is this: When an error has arisen from any transposition of fifiuers, the difference between such transposed number of figures is uniformly a multiple of the numeral nine. For instance, suppose an error occurs in bringing out a trial balance or cash settlement of the amount in question, or that the sum short or over can he divided by nine without any remainder, there is a strong probability that the mistake has been made by transposing figures; at any rate, if such mistake takes place by reason of transposition, the sum in question wili divide by nine without remainder. To illustrate this further: if 97 has been put down 79, the error will be 18, or twice 9 exactly; if 322 be set down 223, the error will he 99, or eleven times 9, and so on between any transposed numbers. This class of errors is very common. þÿ N. T. Courier if Enquirer.

The Clock at St. þÿPaul s, London. þÿ The Pendulum is fourteen feet long, and the weight at the end of it is one hundred weight: the dial on the outside is regulated by a smaller one within ; the length of the minute hand on ihe exterior dials is fifteen feet, and the length of the hour hand is eight feet, and the weight of each seventy-five pounds; the length of the hour figures two feet and two and a half inches. In the face of the dial is an aperture of about a foot square, through which visitors are allowed to protrude their heads to observe the hands in motion, the minute hand making a considerable leap at each swing of the pendulum. A gentleman was at onetime indulging his curiosity in this way, the hand being above bis head, and afterwards turning to look below, remained in that position, until on attempting to move lie found the minute hand close upon the back of his neck, and was totally unable to extricate himself. In a short time he would have been inevitably suffocated, even if decapitation had not ensued. Fortunately, a friend was with him, who hastily summoned assistance, and the clock was stopped just in time to save his life. Since that time, the guide takes care to caution visitors ngainst prolonging their observations at a certain period in every hour. lip to noon yesterday (the 7th) the European Steamer had not arrived at St. Thomas being then nearly six days overdue at that port. Many are the surmises afloat regarding her absence ; some have attributed her non-arrival to strong head winds and bad weather, others that she must have run short of fuel and was compelled to put into either Fayal or Madeira for a supply,

and others that she may have met with some very serious accident. Of three evils, then, let us chose the least, and hope that by the return of the schooner Vigilant þÿ which left this port to-day þÿ from St. Thomas, we may learn the glad tidings of the þÿPacket s afe arrival there, and also be placed iu possession of some good news from abroad, for really at the present time we are quite devoid of that commodity. From the East (the Crimea, Jj-c.) we look for little or nothing ; but, may-be, we may hear that some amicable understanding has been come to between Great Britain and the United States in regard to the Central American question, which is now occupying the attention of Congress and the British Parliament, and also that the momentous question of the Sound Dues is being speedily settled to the satisfaction of the Governments of the U. S. and the Mother Country. Of the evils of a war between England and America, Mr. Bright, Member of Parliament, says : þÿ þÿ Many of us have relatives or friends in America. That voung nation lias a population about equal to ours. It has a great internal and external commerce. It has more tonnage in shipping than we have. It lias more railroads than we have. It has more newspapers than we have. It has more free institutions than we have þÿ that horrid slavery of the South excepted þÿ -aud which is no fruit of its institutions, hut an unhappy legacy of the past. It has also a great manufacturing interest in different branches. That is the young

giant whose shadow ever grows, and there is the true rival of this country. How do we stand or start in the race ? The United States Government, including all the Governments of all the Sovereign States, raises in taxes probably from £12,000,000 to £15,000,000 sterling in the year. England this year will raise and will expend nearly £100,000,000. This population must raise and will expend, probably, £80,000, 000 within this year more than that population will raise and spend, and iu America there is far less poverty aud pauperism than in England. Can we run this race on these terms and against these odds ? Can wc hope to be as well off as America if the products of our industry arc thus swept away, and in the vain scheme of saving Europe from imaginary dangers ? Can poverty bo lessened among us, can education spread, can the brutality of so many of our population be uprooted, can all or anything that good men look for come to us, while the fruits of our industry, the foundation of all social and moral good are squandered in this manner r Pursue the phantom of military glory for ten years and expend in that time a sum equal to all the visible property of Lancashire and Yorkshire, and then compare yourself with the United States of America, and where will you be ? Pauperism, crime, and political anarchy arc the legacies we are preparing for our children, and there is no escape for us unless we change our course, and resolve to disconnect ourselves from the policy which
tends incessantly to embroil us with the nations of the continent of þÿEurope.

Cholera in Porto Kiro ! Bv the schooner Reserve., Captain George, from St. Thomas yesterday, we are in receipt of the þÿ þÿTidende of the 2nd instant from that Island, containing accounts from Porto Rico to the 30th January, þÿ which we subjoin. The same paper furnishes a detail of the deaths occasioned by Cholera ; these amount in the aggregate, from the 1 1 tli November 1855, to the 21st January 1856, to Five thousand two hundred and five throughout the Islaud. The official statistics before us shew that the district of Arccibo has suffered the greatest mortality ; of 1302 cases 1018 proved fatal, out of a population of 15,342 inhabitants. Twenty-live towns and villages, in all, were infected with the scourge

Happily, however, the Epidemic was believed to be assuming a milder type. The þÿ lidcnde remarks : þÿ þÿ the steamer Derwent, which arrived on By Thursday morning from St. þÿJohn s, Porto Rico, we have come in possession of dates from the north side of the Island to the 30th, and from the south to the 28th ultimo. We are happy to say that the districts of Guayatna, Ponce, Mayaguez and Aguadilla are reported healthy, and Planters had availed themselves ot the favorable change of weather to cut and grind ; not, however, without many fears of the Cholera making its appearance among them at their busiest time , fears grounded in the prevailing belief that the expressed juice of the sugar cane is, from its relaxing qualities, a great promoter of the mysterious epidemic. Sugars were quoted at $4jJ and $1 j. Coffee at $12jj. þÿ The Cholera had not advanced farther than the village of Hatillo, eight miles west of Arecibo, and not less than thirty miles from Aguadilla. þÿ In the Island of Porto Rico the peasants, who are a mixture of the aboriginal Caribs and the Spanish settlers, are freemen of ludicrously independent character ; they are indolent and superstitious, but polite and hospitable, and are subject to scarcely any other authority than that of the Alcade de Barrio, or country Bailiff, who is, in most cases, a poor shop-keeper in a neighbouring hamlet. From the luxuriance of the soil in an island where nature teems with the growth of tropical vegetation, the Gibaro, as the

native of Porto Rico is called, neither works nor wants ; but awaits in a state of sweet-do-nothing, a turn of fortune, to come either from his patron Saint or his favorite Virgin. His capital consists in the invariable þÿauxiliary a cutlass ; and not unfrequently a wretched looking mare þÿ his yegua karagan The peasants do not live together in villages as the higher classes, nor do they live together in pent-up plantations as the slaves are compelled to do, but, as many of our readers know, they arc scattered iu isolated huts over the whole length and breadth of the land, from Oeiha to Cabo-rojo, at a distance sometimes of twelve or fifteen miles from any considerable town. Their palm-houses, with occasionally an adjoining field of tobacco or a waving patch of corn, are to be seen alike on the mountains of Luquillo, Cayey, or Aibonito, as in the valleys of Rio Grande, Adjuntas, or Anasco. Hence, the difficulty of arriving at a correct estimate of the number of cases, or the numbet of victims of Cholera. þÿ We have, nevertheless, all reason to believo that the fearful disease is decreasing in the island, and very fervently hope that it will not reach the village of Quebradillas, half-way between Arecibo and Aguadilla, which it now þÿthreatens.

The <k Tennessee þÿ! Tut; United States Mail Steam-ship Tennessee, Captain Johnson, arrived here on Wednesday morning, after a passage of fifty-eight hours from La Guayra. I his vessel met with a most unpardonable detention at the ports of La Guayra and Porto Cabello, and no belter luck has attended her here, for she laid in port fifty-eight hours to exchange mails, take coals, freight and passengers. She ai rivad here from New York on the 16th ult., and has occupied sixteen days in making the voyage to Venezuela and hack, and taking her final departure hence. It requires hut a few figures to tell that with a continuation of such despatch, what will he the termination of this project. The Yankees are proverbial for the go-ahead principle, but if fifty-eight, hours arc to be absorbed alongside a wharf to receive 100 tons of coal,

3T, Q '& b 1'JL þÿA 3. H which should be the work of six hours, the account current of this ship will soon shew a balance on the wrong side. Time is, indeed, money with steamers, and unless the subsequent voyages ot the Tennessee prove an improvement on her first, no company, however well disposed or wealthy, will be willing to continue the operation. As þÿ despatch is the soul of þÿbusiness, so must every arrangement for steamers be made to avoid delay; there must be no detention to adjust disbursements accounts. The Agents must have the power to examine, and if found correct, pay bills after the departure of a ship þÿ for her time must not be lost on trifles, even at the risk of paying a small bill twice over. Coal carriers must be employed and got ready at the wharf as soon as the steamer is signalled, and six hours should suffice at any port of call. From the foregoing remarks we do not infer that any one connected with the steamer, whether on board or ashore, has been remiss in his duty, or wanting in energy, to afford that despatch so essentially needed ; we only intend, ar- by these suggestions, to shew that rangements must be entered into for the future in such manner as to avoid delay, i. e., if a steam communication from the United States in South America is seriously meditated, otherwise it will soon conclude by finding the steamers occupied on the line quietly moored on the placid waters of the Hudson. þÿ St. Thomas Times, February 2.

Port of Spain Gazette, of the 19th January, supplies the following further particulars connected with the late Hank forgeries committed in that Island : þÿ the following advertisement in one put The investigation connected with this untoward occurrence : the examination of persons whose testimony might throw light upon the mystery; and the following up those clues which promise any in way to elucidate the subject and bring home the guilt to the perpetrators of the fraud þÿ are not yet terminated. Sufficient grounds of suspicion, however, have been discovered to justify the incarceration of two persons namely, the Dominican servant of Mr. Gordon þÿ Thomas, and a man called Gabou or Bodu þÿ a petty dealer trafficing between the stores in town and purchasers from the Spanish Main. The suspicions against the former are rather of a culminating amount of slight circumstances, unimportant, taken separately and singly ; but which form on the whole a very sufficing array of criminating circumstances. The latter is, we understand, identified by the cashier, Mr. Brown, by the porter William, and by other persons who had business at the Bank on that morning, as the person to whom the checque, purporting to be drawn by Mr. P. B. Andre, was paid ; and it is stated that he endorsed the checque by writing his name across the back. We undestand that he admits having received cash for a checque about that time, but declares that it was one of Mr. þÿAgostini þÿ s a declaration dis-

proved however, by an examination of that þÿgentleman sBanking book. The discovery of all the missing checques, except the forged ones, in the watercloset of the establishment, would appear to fix the act of securing the passed checques on some one in the place ; apply there being crushed together in a lump,

would seem to intimate that they were taken in the dark from the pigeon holes by a person who knew the relative position of the letters ; the forged ones afterwards picked out to be more certainly destroyed, and these got rid of by the readiest means at hand. It being remembered that, though entry into the Bank by some one who knew the building might be comparatively easy, the appearance of a light at an unusual hour would lie most likely instantly observed, and its cause ascertained. But if we begin to speculate on possibilities and appearances, there might he much difficulty in bringing our observations to a close ; the field is very extensive, but as the Reporter clearly proves iu its impression of this morning, its cultivation very barren in results. We leave the matter, therefore, with out farther comment. By Wednesday, we trust the results of the examination þÿ very properly kept secret while the investigation is going on þÿ will be finished, and then there can be no scruple in laying all the facts of the case before tee Public.

þÿPoets Corner. þÿ þÿRELIGION WHAT IS þÿIT? þÿ Is it to go to church to-day, To look devout and seem to pray, And ere þÿto-morrow sun s goes down, Be dealing slander through the town 3 þÿ Does every sanctimonious face Denote the certain reign of grace 3 Does not a phiz that scowls at sin Oft veil hypocrisy within 3 þÿ Is it to make our daily walk, And of our own good deeds to talk, Vet often practice secret crime, And thus rais-spend our precious time 3 þÿ Is it for sect and creed to fight, To call our zeal the rule of right, When what we wish is, at the best. To see our church excel the rest 3

þÿ Is it to wear the Christian dress. And love to all mankind profess, To treat with scorn the humble poor. And bar against them every door ? þÿ no Oh, ; Religion means not this ; Its fruit more sweet and fairer is Its precept this þÿ þÿ To others do As you would have them do to þÿyou. þÿ It grieves to hear an ill report, And scorns with human woes to sport. Of þÿothers deeds it speaks no ill, But. tells of good, or else keeps still. þÿ And does religion this impart 3 Then may its influence fill my heart, Oh, haste the blissful, joyful day, When all the earth shall own its sway þÿ!

MINERAL SUBSTANCES IN PLANTS. Nitrogen is abundant in the sap of young plants, eventually becoming fixed plentifully in the seeds and young leaves. Potash and soda circulate in the sap, and fix themselves in the green fleshy leaves and in bulbous roots, Sulphuric acid, abundant where the potash and soda are. Phosphoric acid fixing itself in the seeds and reproductive parts of plants. Lime in the sap, depositing itself in the leaves and bark, and in some seeds and roots. Magnesia in the sap, becoming fixed in the seeds. Chlorine, chiefly with the soda. Silica in the sap, in a soluble form, becoming deposited chiefly in the exterior portion of the stems and leaves, giving strength to the plant. Flint is found on the exterior of all the graminaceous order, and produces the polished surface of the canepalm. Sulphur abounds in cruciferous plants ; especially in mustard. Copper in coffee, wheat etc. ; and iron in tobacco, and in the fruit of the strawberry.

The Courier des Etats Unis says : þÿ þÿ It is a long vaulted room, with a large bow window, hung with a light drapery, the lower half covered with reen silk curtains, like those in a þÿpainter studio. s A table and chair of ordinary appearance are before it þÿ the table covered with books and papers; here and there a sofa of the straight form, which was fashionable at the beginning of the century ; a large chair hardly more comfortable, some wooden backed ones of a smaller size, and a few modest stands, are placed about the room. On the walls are pictures, portraits, prints, tokens of affection, souvenirs. The prirciple article of furniture, if it may lie called so, is a camp bed, which seems formed of eight bars of simple wood, supporting a box, on which is laid a single mattress. The most common hospital lied seems more comfortable, a real þÿsoldier bed, s a dying þÿman trundle. s The Emperor died there, wrapped in a military cloak, as if a bullet had suddenly struck him at the head of his army. 'This remarkable simplicilv corresponds little with the desire for pomp and power which prevails at the North ; hut at this solemn conjuncture, does not simplicity seem real grandeur? that is, the little that is given to man here below. The Emperor-Pope dying on a little wooden bed, in the immense winter palace of his enormous capital, and coolly employing the telegraph to write to the second city of his empire. þÿ The Emperor

bids farewell to þÿMoscow þÿ this warlike Czar giving, himself, his directions for his modest funeral obsequies, dictating the political documents þÿ in which lie speaks of himself as already dead þÿ this powerful despot not once saying, þÿ I þÿwill, in his solemn testament hut only, þÿ þÿdesire, I þÿ þÿbeg, I þÿ all this impresses the mind, as the view of this dwelling strikes the eye, giving to the narrative something unexpected and striking ; in the midst of which we forget the fever of international events; to see only the father of his family departing from them, and a soul leaving the þÿworld.

Man is so much the creature of habit as regards food, that he makes little or scarcely any provision for a scarcity of any of the particular articles of diet to which he has been accustomed. He abandons himself to despair and violence instead of profiting by his experience. In the present day there ought to be no | such tiiiriff as a famine, or even high prices. Nature is not exhausted. Within her fertile boson there may lie thousands of substances, yet unknown, as precious as the only recently found gutta perclia. To doubt this, would be to repudiate the most logical inference afforded by the whole history of the larth. Corn and grape excepted, nearly all our staples in vegetable product are of comparatively modern discovery. Society had a long existence without tea, coffee, cotten, cocoa, sugar and potatoes. Who shall say there is not a more nutritious plant than the þÿ than the potato a more useful tree than sugar-cane þÿ a finer root the cotton? Buried wealth lise everywhere in the bowels of the earth, which needs but the true divining rod of organized action for its discovery.

The Packet ! The long-looked-for Packet of the 17th January, after being overdue eight days, has at length arrived þÿ removing all conjecture as

to her safety. The schooner Vigilant, Higgins, returned from St. Thomas on Sunday afternoon with our mails. We learn that the outward steamer þÿ Parana þÿ experienced veryheavy weather and adverse winds, which caused her to run short of coal, and she was compelled to put into Madeira to replenish supply. It is said she was detained at that port for about four days. The intelligence by this ship is vague and unimportant, as our extracts will shew : þÿ DENMARK. Intelligence from Hamburg states that the Danish Government has just sent a circular to the different States of Europe. In this circular the Danish Government renews the declaration of neutrality. Denmark persists in maintaining the position of a neutral Power, and admits no engagements on its side in relation to the treaty concluded on the 21st of November between Sweden and the Western Powers.

The Berlin correspondent of the þÿ þÿTimes says : þÿ þÿ According to a private letter I have received from Copenhagen, it is stated that the Danish government, under the twofold pressure of the partial relinquishment of neutrality by Sweden, and the apparently inevitable conflict with the United States, on account of the Sound dues, has decided upon making advances to the Allies in the matter of the future campaign in the Baltic. For some time the government, as is represented to me, wavered between England and France, to which of the two it should make its advances, and at last decided for the former ; in consequence of which a special envoy is very shortly to be accredited to London for the purpose of concluding a treaty, by which England shall guarantee to Denmark the possession of her West India Islands. In case of hostilities breaking out between the United States and Denmark, which would naturally result from any United States vessel attempting to pass the Sound without paying the dues, it is apprehended by the Danes that the first step taken by the Americans would be to lay violent hands on the Danish Island of St. Thomas. The recent expedition of British naval forces to the West Indies, as explained by our government to have taken place for the purpose of protecting our own territories there from piratical invasion, will throw an appearance of probability upon the idea that our government may fall in with this þÿview.

THE SOUND DUES. The latest advices from Copenhagen state that the Danisli government had fixed the 28th December for tlie opening of the conference on the Sound Dues, but that, at the request of several representatives of foreign Powers, this term was postponed to the 2nd of January, for which it now remains fixed.

The Brussels j journal has even heard that the language employed in the document denotes a remarkable change in þÿSweden relations s with Russia, and is of so marked a character as to justify the belief chief of St. Thomas Militia Jaeger Corps, as j that in the Spring she will engage energetically in the war. YVc learn from a good source (says the Nuremberg correspondent) that, besides the treaty of Nov. 21, there are in existence special conventions between the Western Powers and Sweden These acts were prepared during the stay of General Canrobert at Stockholm. They remain still to be ratified, and will not be published un- ! less hostilities against Russia should continue in
the Spring. These conventions will place Sweden in an entirely new attitude to Russia, and will have for their effect much more than to concede depot 8 and stations to the allied fleets.

The Swedish journal, Faedrelandet , reports, under date Stockholm, Dec. 24 : þÿ Activity unducing articles necessary to the equipment exampled reigns in every manufactory for ot pro- an army. The colonels of all the regiments have received orders to supply their troops with everything necessary to prepare them for marching at the first signal. The order was given secretly, but it was in its nature impossible of concealment. All leaves of absence to officers are refused. Everybody here believes that in case the Allies should open the war with vigour in the Baltic next spring, our government will feel itself compelled to take an active part therein.

THE COUNCIL OF WAR AT PARIS. The Monileur publishes the following : þÿ þÿ A Council of War met to-day at the Tuileries. 'flic Emperor presided. The Council is composed of the Emperor, the Prince Jerome Napoleon, the Duke of Cambridge, Prince Napoleon, Lord Cowley, Sir Edmund Lyons, Admiral Dundas, Sir Richard Airey, Sir Harry Jones, General La Marmora, Marshal Vaillant, Count Walewski, General Canrobert, General Bosquet, Gener.l Niel, General Martinique', Admiral Hamelin, Admiral Jarier de la Graviere and Admiral Penaud. THE PEACE PROPOSALS. Berlin, Thursday Evening. It has been stated here that Count Stakelberg is on his way from St Petersburg to Vienna with the answer to the Austrian propositions. The reply of Russia to the propositions will be sent to Vienna direct, and not handed to Count Esterhazy. The return reply from Austria must go to St. Petersburg, to Count Esterhazy, to be by him handed to Count Nesselrode. This mode of transmission will create delay. The object is not at present apparent, but Russia purposes to gain all possible time. England is taking a very high tone towards this Government. The blockade is threatened to be extended to the Prussian ports. The Cabinet is becoming alarmed, and strong efforts will be made to induce Russia to accede to the terms proposed. Another telegraph dispatch says þÿ þÿ Count Stackelberg left St. Petersburg Tuesday even- on ing, as soon as he was well enough to travel. The statements in reference to the negotiations are very contradictory. Count Nesselrode is said to have declared confidentially that, in his opinion, Russia had conceded all she ought to do by her circular of the 22nd ultimo. According to the Konigsberg Gazette, Russia has declined the mediation of Austria, and accepts that of Saxony From Vienna the report is that Count Nesselrode has declared the propositions of the 22nd December present no absolute character, and that Russia expects and admits modifications to be þÿoffered. nounces that the Russian reply to the propositions conveyed to St. Petersburg by Count Valentine Esterhazy has been delivered by Prince Gortscbakoff The spirit of this reply is conciliatory, and pacific sentiments are expressed. It does not contain a full and unreserved acceptance of the propositions ; but the objections being mostly formal, hopes of attaining the desired object may still be entertained. Berlin, Jan. 1 1 . The Wife of the Present Emperor of Russia. þÿ A letter from Paris, in the Manchester Guardian, says : þÿ þÿ The Czarewitch Alexander, as you may remember, married for love, and not for any political consideration, espousing one of the loveliest but poorest and least important of German Princesses, the daughter of the Grand Duke of Hesse Darmstadt. For many reasons the Czar was ill-disposed towards the marriage, but his son would hear of no other, and the father ended by yielding. The Princess Marie of Darmstadt left her þÿfather most s dull and impoverished court, and a home where she had tasted but few joys of any kind, for the most splendid of Northern capitals, where the second place was to be hers. Her own position was a happy one, but between her father-inlaw and herself there reigned, for the first few months, small affection. He took little or no notice of her, aad she made no apparent efforts to win his favour þÿ above all, made no obsequious advances towards him. When the day anticipated that with the vast resources of St. Nicholas came round, the þÿCzar s fete day, the reigning Empress and Princesses were much astonished to find that alone, of all the family, the Czarewna, as the wife of the heir apparent is styled, took no part in the various little works that each member of it made a point of getting ready in order to present them its chief. No remark, however, was made on either side, and the day came. The presents were given and accepted, and when all was over the Grand Du-

chess Marie rose from her place, advanced towards the Czar, and sinking before him on one knee, with an air of great reverence repeated the long Credo of the Greek Church, from the first word to the last, in Russian, and with the purest pronunciation. The Czar, comprehending instantaneously what a force ofwilland application had been required to render possible this feat (the Princess having been ignorant of a single Russian word but a few months before), rapturously embraced his daughter-in law, and from that hour really, and not took her to bis þÿheart.

It was found necessary to amputate the leg, for which purpose his Lordship was conveyed to the village of Waterloo, where, in the house of a draper, the operation was successfully performed ; and the amputated limb was buried iu the garden of the draper, and over the spot he has planted a weeping willow The following epitaph was written some years since, for the tablet : þÿ Here rests þÿ and let no saucy knave Presume to sneer or laugh, To learn that mouldering in the grave Is laid þÿ a British calf ;
For he who writes these lines is sure That those who read the whole Will find such laugh were premature. For here, too, lies a sole.
And here five little ones repose, Twin-born with other five, Unheeded by their brother toes. Who all are now alive.
A leg and foot to speak more plain, , Lie here of one commanding ; Who, though his wits he might retain, Lost half his understanding
Who, when the guns with thunder fraught Poured bullets thick as hail, Could only in this way be taught To give the foe leg-bail.
And now in England, just as gay As in the battle brave, Goes to the rout, review, or play. With one foot in the grave.
Fortune in vain here showed her spite, For he will still be found, Should þÿEngland sons s engage in fight, Prepared to stand, his ground.
But þÿFortune pardon s I must bear , She meant not to disarm ; And when she lopped the þÿhero leg, s By no means sought his h-arm ;
And but indulged a harmless whim, Since ho could walk with one ; She saw two legs were lost on him. Who never meant to run.

HAVE CHARITY FOR THE POOR. Rich men and rich ladies, whom God has mercifully blessed with the good things of this world, have mercy on the poor, for they are vour fellow beings. They toil and struggle in the tough battle of life. They toil long and struggle hard to gain a scanty supply of food for themselves and their little ones. They are roughlookiDg, but kind-hearted one toward another. They have sympathetic hearts like our own, with this difference, that we, so far placed above and beyond them by the voice of fashion, do not so readily give from our abundance as they to their comrades from the dry crusts which they have begged at our gates Have charity, then þÿ have compassion upon the poor who are about you. Who knows how soon the wheel of fortune may turn round and crush us in its ceaseless motion ? As high as wc stand to-day, we may be brought low and suffering to morrow ; therefore, tn-day. have charity for the poor '

THE RIGHT TO KEEP BIRDS AND ANIMALS. A case was tried in the Exeter County Court on Tuesday þÿ Abraham v. þÿMinty, to test the right of persons to keep birds and animals, which, by crowing and harking, proved an annoyance to their neighbours. The defendant kept a dog ; for the protection of his premises, and also reared poultry. The allegation on the part of the plaintiff was that he suf- I for Kjolmiand Thomas James til vod fered annoyance f rom the harking of the dog, and particularly from t he loud and incessant crowing of a bantam fowl, ( which crowed six or seven times in the course of a minute. The damages for j this annoyance were laid at £\. The Judge, Mr. J. Tyrrell, held that persons in towns and villages had no right to keep animals which annoyed their neighbours, hut at the same time the latter must not he too exacting. No one would complain of an occasional hark or crow, hut he thought no biped would require to crow 150 times in 25 minutes, and that no reasonable person was hound to put up with so much crowing, i He, therefore, inflicted the nominal penalty of one shilling for the crowing i in the month of September, and said that an action might he brought for the crowing of every day in the year. þÿ Lon- , don Paper.

Monday, the 28th of January, 1856, the Burgher Council held its ordinary meeting at the usual time and place. The Vice-Chairman absent. The following cases referred : Letters and communications from Government : þÿ For Council's information, that the now measurement of the buildings in this island is to be used as a guide for compiling the Landtreasury's Matrieul for 1855, and that lots of the estates in the vicinity of the towns must not be entered as town lots, except by especial approval of the Government. Orders issued to accountant. Forwarding for Council's opinion a report transmitted by the Committee appointed to propose what repairs are wanted to the Courthouse in the town of Christiansted ; Government observe, that it would be very expedient to have all the offices in one and the same building, and recommends for this purpose to purchase the adjoining property No. 11 King street. Circulated for the deliberation of the members. Fo> Council's information, that the Chief Inspector of Roads had been requested to have trees planted along the new road purchased from the estate Prosperity, Westend quarter, for the protection of said road in the event of great washes. Council also reminded of the contents of Government's letter respecting the remuneration due the owners for the piece of land in question. That in consequence of the continuous cases of yellow fever among the garrison, it has been proposed to remove the patients during the repairs of the military hospital to the wards for the

Landtreasury's patients, and as the said repairs are so far advanced, the patients in question may be moved back in the course of a fortnight provided the contemplated painting be postponed for a few months ; in consequence whereof Council issued the necessary orders in said respect. Requesting Council to appoiut two Planters to convene with the Custom-house Officers to report to Government the prices of produce to be used as a guide for fixing the tariff, pursuant whereto Messrs. Arnesen and Newton were nominated Forwarding the declaration of the Master of Police at Christiansted regarding the subject of the Night Watch, requesting Council to convene with said official for the purpose of deliberating upon and reporting to Government if a Night Watch ought to be and in what manner it might he established in said town. This case circulates for deliberation among the members, after which the needful will be attended to. That in consequence of a representation from the Chief Inspector of Roads, the purchase of a piece of cane-land belonging to estate La Vallee had been considered necessary to be used as public road instead of that part that runs along the sea, this being pronounced by a Committee to be useless and dangerous, and the remuneration fixed at $50. The framing of the road to be done by assessment on the estates in the quarter, the work however to be postponed until the standing canes arc cut off. The within amount assigned. sal of the Hospital Commission at Christiansted to erect a dead-house at the south western corner of the burial ground, according to estimate to

EURO PEAN. The Nord , of Brussels, publisbshes the follow- " The government has just taken a resolution of the highest importance, which I hasten tocomraunicate to you. You are aware that for some time it has been invited, even urged, by France and England to conclude with them a treaty similar to that concluded with Sweden, which would assure the territorial integrity of Denmark against any eventual eucroachtnent ou the part of Russia. Having maturely deliberated upon this question our Government has just in a positive manner declined all offer of guarantee on the part of the Western Powers against chimerical eventualities, and in which in reality those Powers no more believe than we do. " The Minister of Foreign Affairs has addressed to all European Governments, under date of 4th of January, a circular, in which our Government, after referring to the declaration of Sweden, which has just again announced her strict neutrality despite the treaty of 21st of November last with France and England, brings forward three points as the principle of the policy it is resolved to maintain, and which will serve as its guide in its relations with other nations as long as the present war lasts. " By the first point Denmark renews the declaration to Europe, that wishing to maintain her attitude of strict neutrality towards the belligerent Powers, she declines any share of responsibility in the obligations which the treaty of the 21st of November might eventually entail upon Sweden towards one of the two Western Powers. Denmark wishes in this respect to maintain her full

freedom of action, without in any manner following Sweden on the new political ground upon which she might be led in virtue of the clauses of the treaty of the 21st of November. By the second point, our Government also renews to the foreign Powers its very formal declaration of remaining totally neutral in the European conflict, of taking no active part therein, cither by giving a contingent of land forces, or by her fleet, in favour of any of the belligerent Powers ; that is to say, that we shall not depart in anv respect from that pacific attitude of strict neutrality which we imposed upon ourselves bv the treaty concluded in February, 1853, with Sweden. " By the third point of the circular the Minister of foreign Affairs proclaims a grand principle of international law, namely, that the King of Denmark is at liberty as Sovereign of a free and independent State to adopt that line of conduct he may deem best suited to the interests of the Danish nation, whilst observing at the same time towards the other nations of Europe the same relations of friendship and goodwill as heretofore. Desirous of enjoying the plenitude of sovoreign power we shall always know how to respect scrupulously the political interests of other nations. " You will observe (adds the Nord) that the note of Denmark, which appears to be nothing more than the reproduction of the joint declaration made in virtue of the Treaty with Sweden

3 X S H Z H A T I 5 of 1853, acquires, however, an additional importance as well on accout of the coming campaign in the Baltic, for which such formidable preparations are being made in France and England, as also from the impression the recent treaty of Sweden with the Western Powers may have caused in Europe."

FRANCE, The Paris correspondent of the Times says: þÿ "I understand that the assurance was again given to-day in an official quarter of the resolution of this Government to carry on the war in the most vigorous manner in the event of Russia not acceding to the propositions adopted by the allies. It was repeated at the same time that the Emperor Napoleon ing, under date of Copenhagen, January 7 : þÿ had no insatiable desire for war, on the contrary, he would feel as much satisfaction as any one that the war should cease hut that he and the English Government were determined not to abate one iota of the terms on which peace would he accepted, and that if Russia still held out, she will soon see how two such Powers make war in the Baltic. It was not decided that there was still a glimmer of hope of peace, hut it was admitted that the glimmer was very faint indeed. This does not differ in any respect from what I have more than once described as the disposition of the French Government, hut it is no harm to repeat each time that counter statements appear in the Russian press of Belgium and Germany.

RELATIONS BETWEEN PRUSSIA AND GREAT BRITAIN. The Correspondence du Danube has the the following communication dated Berlin, Jan. 4. þÿ "It has often been said that the relations of the Cabinet of Berlin with the Cabinet of the Tuileries are much more satisfactory than those maintained with the Cabinet of St. James's. Recently a tact has occurred, which proves that Prussia's relations with England leave mueh to be desired. It appears that the Earl of Clarendon has had at London an interview with Count de Bemstorff', the Prussian Ambassador, in which the role of Prussia in the Eastern question has been discussed. The Earl of Clarendon, in this interview, spoke in no equivocal terms of the neutrality of Prussia; he complained that Prussia continues to send lare quantities of war material to Russia, and that the Prussian Government, in tolerating this state of things, lends a hand to the enemy of France and England. The Earl of Clarendon, moreover, expressed his surprise that superior officers of the Prussian army should have assisted at the fete organised by the Russian am< bassador at Berlin in celebration of the surrender of Kars, and that the name of Kars had been used after the taking of that fortress as a not d'ordre at a review at Berlin, as if the Russians had achieved a glorious victory for the arms of Prussia. Even if England, continued the Earl of Clarendon, were not to see in all these facts so many demonstrations in favour of Russia, it could not avoid observing the indifference with which Pr ussia sustains her moral co-operation.

England will find itself, then, compelled to take some serious, and even hostile measures, if the Cabinet of Berlin does not see fit to change its attitude. The Ambassador of Prussia has addressed to his Government a confidential dispatch, containing a very detailed account ot this interview. This dispatch arrved at the time M. de Manteuffel was at

Lusace, but he returned to Berlin immediately on hearing of Count BernstorfTs dispatch. The Council of Ministers assembled under the presidency of the King at Charlottenburg, and the communications made by the Earl of Clarendon to the Prussian Ambassador at London were much discussed. Although the declarations of England have produced a profound impression here, it does not seem that Prussia will make any attempts to prevent the measures complained ot by the English Minister. It is believed that there is a question of the eventual blockade of the Prussian ports in the Baltic. The rumour of the possible concentration of the French army upon the Rhine has made a sensation, and it lias been suggested to interdict the circulation in Prussia of the Gazette d'Augsbourg, which first published the report. " It is known here, from the best sources, that Sweden is preparing for participation in the great events of which the shores of the Baltic will be the theatre in the approaching spring. The armaments of Sweden and Norway are being pushed forward with great energy."

Wounds at the Cavalrv Charge. þÿ At a medical board, held on Friday, at Brompton, among the number passed as unfit for further service was Robert Evans, 13th Light Dragoons, a youth, who has been in hospital nearly twelve months, and received his injury in an extraordinary manner. In the charge of Balaklava a shell entered the chest of his horse, which rolled completely over, falling upon Evans, when the shell burst inside the animal, tearing it open from the shoulder to the hind-quarters, the weight of the horse nearly causing suffocation, while its death struggle inflicted severe contusions on the legs of Evans, who would soon have expired had not a man of his troop and two lancers released him. Her Majesty evinced great sympathy for the youth, and his photograph likeness was taken by her special command.

EXTRAORDINARY STORY It appears that during the stay of the Persian ambassador in Moscow a fire of charcoal, lighted by his servant in a stove of the room where his son and the servant slept, caused the death of the former by suffocation, while the latter narrowly escaped with his life. The ambassador, in order to avenge the death of his son, commanded the ser vant, to whose carelessness the accident was attributed, to be flayed alive. The Russian police, however, interfered, alleging that such a punishment could not be allowed in their country. Accordingly his Excellency ordered a box with airholes to be made, for the purpose of transporting lis unfortunate, servant to Persia, there to suffer the fearful death which even Russian civilization prohibited ! A Soldier Flogged to Death. The correspondent of the Morning Herald, in his letter from the Crimea, dated Dec. 24, says : þÿ " A private of the English Artillery has this week died under the lash at Balaklava. I believe his offence was drunkenness. Be it so. Are there no roads to he made or mended ? Are there no stones to he broken ? Are there no round shot to be polished ? Is it not better to stop grog than to stop life t Let your readers answer. My opinion is that ihough in many cases, such as mutiny or desertion, flogging is admissible, it (now that the enemy does not harass us, now that men can well be spared for sentries over prisoners), is not the best punishment for drunkenness. I shall not argue this question out now, I shall simplysay that this private was made fast to the usual limberwheel, that his state was apparently not one of health, that he was sentenced to receive, and did receive in full, 50 lashes, at the hands of the serjeant-farrier of the left siege-train at Balaklava Heights, and that on being cast loose he fell to the ground like a log, there remained a short time, was carried to the hospital, and there died. I am told that this private belonged to the 8th company of the 7th battalion (Royal Artillery), hut I have failed as yet to learn his name. He died on Sunday morning (yesterday), having been flogged on Saturil y, after the departure of the last mail from Balaklava ; and I think that the War-office authorities ought to investigate the case.
Men are men, and must not he treated as beasts, for which latter we have, at i least, a ' Martin's Act.' "

Government's letter approving of the building of a prison in the courtyard at Frederiksted, cost S400, and requesting Council to take again into deliberation the proposal to move the Brand-depot from the hospital to the Courtyard, cost estimated at $308 47. The needful communication regarding said prison building will be issued to the Master of Police, who in conjunction with another member were charged with the inspection of this work. Our member for Frederiksted, the Master of Police, having observed, that the spot which was once fixed upon for the erection of the Brand-depot had since been applied for other purposes, and as Council could not suppose that there exists any reasonable objections to the Brand-depot remaining where it is, it was agreed upon, to forward a representation to this effect to Government, and thus obviate an additional expense of above S300. W k have much pleasure in announcing that His Lordship the Bishop of Antigua and the Leeward Islands is expected to arrive here from Torlola, in the schooner " Scholten," either this evening or tomorrow morning. The 1st February Packet, due here yesterday, has not arrived up to the time of our preparing for the press ; therefore are we without any later European intelligence than that published in our last. From flic London Weekly Dispatch, LOSS OF THE THEMIS The French journals contain accounts from Eupatoria to the 24th of December. The garrison made frequent promenades, and any Russians that were seeu always retreated at their advance. The Turks lately captured two Cossacks, who had lost their way in a fog. According to the statements of these men the Russians are well supplied with provisions, with the exception of meat, which is only served out at rare intervals. I here only remains 2,300 Egyptians at Eupatoria, aud they are almost all in hospital, as the climate d ins not agree with them. The Ottoman troops are well supplied with every thing in the shape ot warm clothing. The Themis, English transport, has just been destroyed by fire She had been chartered by the French Government She had on board 50,000 projectiles and 30,000 of cartridges, and several barrels of powder, for Euputoria. From the moment the fire was discovered no hope of saving ber was entertaiiied, aud attention was exclusively turned to removing the other vessels out ot danger. The cxplosiou ou boa.d succeeded each other rapidly, aud coutiuued for some hours, until at length the vessel sunk.

Liverpool, Nov. 10. were one day this week unpacking a port The Custom-house officers of this bale of tobacco in the bonded warehouse, when, on removing the outer covering of raw oxhide, they tound a Racoon, thin, indeed, to emaciation, but still alive. It had existed, probably for months, by nibbling at the raw ox-nidc, which thus at once became its food and prison-house. It has since been allowed more generous fare, and is rapidly recovering from the effects of its long and hungry confinement. þÿ London Evening Mail.

ACT OF EXCOMMUNICATION AT COBLENTZ. On Sunday we were witness of a ceremony which has not been performed for centuries þÿ viz, an excommunication, the subject being M. Sonntag, a merchant at Coblcntz, who was divorced from his first wife, and eight yoars ago was married, by the civil authorities only, to his present one. Last summer M. Sonntag was commanded by the clergy to seperate from bis

wife, and not obeying their decree, be was on Sunday exeommuuieated Dean Kramentz, after preaching a sermon against the civil marriage, put on some other sacredotal garments, and, accompanied by two clergymen bearing wax tapers, read, standing in the middle of the church, the sentence of excommunication against M. Sonntag and his lady. He then extinguished the taper: , saying that the persons named were not worthy to see the day of the Lord, and throwing the candlesticks to the ground, breaking them to pieces, exclaimed, " Let the bells sound the luneral knell !" We immediately beard the sound of bells and the chants for the dead. The dean, in conclusion, proclaimed that no one whomsoever was to hold relations with the excommunicated, to salute them, -c. This prohibition has not had much effect, for their house has been filled ever since with visitors, and at night they have been serenaded. þÿ London Paper

W e make no apology in directing the attention of the þÿpublic particularly the agricultural interest þÿ to the portion of an article published in our columns to-day on the Imphce, treating of its invaluable qualities, the climate and soil to which it is best adapted, and the mode of culture. The remainder of the article will be inserted in our next
IMPHEE, OR HOLCUS SACCHARATUS CULTIVATION ; INCLUDING SOIL, CLIMATE, AND SEASONS.

The Detnorara Gazette, after describing the different varieties of lmphec, which Mr. Wray has discovered and cultivated, proceeds to lav before its readers that þÿgentleman mode s of cultivation, as described by himself. Climate. þÿ It may bo safely stated, as an indisputable fact, that wherever maize or Indian corn will grow and ripen its seed, Imphee will likewise grow and elaborate its juices, so as to be suitable for sugar making ; bearing in mind always, that inasmuch as the Maize comprises varieties which require five months, and others which require only three months, so in like manner does the Imphee include those varieties requiring four and a half months, and others again which ripen in two and a half and three months only. This is a very essential fact to be remembered, in order to adapt, in all cases, the variety to the peculiar character of the locality : and I believe that no explanation, however lengthy, could more accurately define the climate range of the Imphee, than simply classing it with the maize, in this respect. In Northern Europe, and in numerous other parts of the world, no kinds of maize can be profitably cultivated, but those which ripen their seed within ninety days from planting : þÿ and it will be found that in all such localities, no other variety of Imphee can be successfully employed, but such as ripen their juices within the same short period Hut what a truly enormous range does this climatic adaptation give us It comprises, in fact, every country of the earth that j mould, the Imphee delights, and will grow famous-

can afford three months of hot summer weather. 1 ly with sufficient moisture. It docs not even exclude Canada or Russia. Rut as we draw nearer and nearer to the Equator, the gradual lengthening of the summer ; | essentials to the full devclopemcnt of the great season, until, indeed, winter is unknown, affords 1 and the perfect elaboration of its a longer and a longer growing time , so that at

last, instead of one crop, we can obtain two , three , aye, and even four crops in one year. It is evident likewise, that the longer the summer or warm weather extends, the greater scope exists for the cultivation of the larger and more productive varieties, that require a longer time for their perfect development. I he small measure of temporary success which is said to have attended the attempts made in 1785 by Signor Arduino, of Florence, to introduce varieties of the þÿ J Iolcus Saccharatus þÿ into European cultivation, and their ultimate failure and consequent disuse, arose from the simple circumstance of his having unfortunately lighted upon varieties which required too long a period for their perfect maturity, to suit the short and variable summer of Europe. I cannot impress this important point too strongly upon the attention of my readers, for on it, in fine, depends the success or failure of the whole cultivation, for the purposes of sugar manufacture. In tropical climates the planter is, of course, free to choose whichever variety his fancy or his experience in time to come, may lead him to prefer. Nor can any set rule be laid down which he must of necessity follow. It is to be supposed that he will select those particular varieties, which will not only yield him a large return per acre, but will afford him an extended period for his manufacturing operations, instead of all becoming ripe together. Soil. þÿ Imphee will grow well, and produce sugar abundantly, in a great variety of soils ; and

in this respect it is very similar to the real sugarcane ; but amongst the many advantages which it has over its great rival, the perfect immunity that it enjoys from the attack of white ants, is one much too important to be passed over without remark. In the colony of Natal, on the south-east coast of Africa, the a kite ant is as numerous, and fully as destructive, as it is in India, consequently none but lowlyiDg, swampy grounds, can be used in that colony for sugar-cane cultivation. And this fact places a restriction upon its extensive culture in Natal, which no human art can overcome : þÿ but such an affletion does not exteud to the Imphee ; on the contrary, the white ants (although swarming the soil) never touch these plants. I have grown a fine crop of Imphee, on a sandy hill-top, where it would have been utterly impossible to grow sugar-cane on account of the white ants. This seems a small matter to dwell upon, but in reality it is of the utmost importance to Natal, India generally, the Straits (Malacca) Settlements, and to every other country whereiu that insect scourge exists ; because it admits of sugar being produced from the Imphee on millions and millions of acres, which are totally unsuited for the sugar-cane. This simple fact alone is calculated to enhance the price of land in Natal and the Cape colony to an immense extent, and it will have the same effect in many other countries. I have introduced the subject of white ants in this place because, in treating of soils suitable

for the sugar-cane, it is absolutely necessary to exclude all those infested by white ants, whereas, in the culture of the Imphee their presence is of no consequence. In rich alluvial soils, in good light brick mould, in loamy soils and indeed in almost every good j soil in which there is an admixture of vegetable
Plenty of vegetable mould, strong heat and light, and considerable moisture, form the plant, juice, so as to yield its maximum quantity of saccharine matter.

If after a season of long-continued showery weather a period of dry weather occurs, just as it ripens, then the juice is more especially abundant and rich in sugar. Soils highly manured with animal manures, or in fact, with any which abound in ammonia and other saline substances tend to the formation of I a large luxurious þÿplant but its juice is so mucilaginous and saline, that it is extremely unsuitable for sugar manufacture : hence such treatment should be studiously avoided. The same rule applies in the case of the sugar-cane, beetroot, and all other sugar-yielding þÿplants and if it be violated the result is certain to be disappointment and vexation. Mode of Culture. þÿ I have in some instances soaked the seed of the Imphee for twenty-four and even forty-eight hours in warm water, previous to planting them, in order to expedite their germination, as seeds so treated will, in warm, moist weather, be up in four days afterwards ; whereas being planted (during showery weather) without this assistance, they usually take six or seven days sprouting. If, after planting, dry weather sets in, they will, however, require ten and even fourteen days to appear above ground þÿ but by being well soaked before hand, this casualty is materially þÿobviated hence, I hold the practice to be a prudent one. The seed requires to be very lightly covered, for if deeply set it is liable to rot, should much rain occur immediately after ; but, lightly covered , it will not be injured by even constant rain.

I have lost a great deal of seed by planting too deeply, and I shall therefore be very cautious never to commit the same error again. If soaked in warm water twenty-four hours, then planted in a bed and care taken to keep them properly moist, we may always calculate to a certainty on having them an inch above ground in four days (warm weather). This first start is a great point, wherever the warm weather last only a short time ; but in no case is it altogether unimportant ; and it becomes a question of no small moment, whether in England, and in some parts of Northern Europe, it would not even be quite worth while to sow seed under glass in the first instance and then plant out the young plants before they are a month old, in the open ground, where it is intended they shall remain for crop. In this case very little more labor is required than is now universally bestowed, on the Conti" nent, in making the beet root nursery -beds, and subsequent transplanting of the young beets. My own experience this season, in England, has shown me, that even in a small green-house, a a prodigious number of young plants may be so raised, without any artificial heat whatever ; and the plants are so hardy, that they hear trans planting admirably. E U R 0 P E A N. RECEPTION OF THE PEACE NEWS AT EUPATORIA. The following is an extract of a letter from Eupatoria of the Dili published by the Constitvtionnel : þÿ þÿ A letter from Eupatoria of the 9th mentions the consternation into which the Tartar population of that place have been thrown by the news of the prospect of peace, which will probably expose them to the most severe retaliatory measures on the part of the Russians. It is the same in the valley of Haidar, at Kertcli, and wherever the allied armies have come into contact with the native population. Within 48 hours

after the allies landed at Enpatoria, 35,000 Tartars, men, women and children, with 10,000 horses, 4.000 or 5,000 carts, 150,000 sheep and nearly 50,000 head of other cattle, came into Eupatoria, where there were before not more than 12,000 inhabitants. Their object, of course, was to fly from the Russians, whose vengeance they feared from hav ing received the allies in a friendly manner. From 3,000 to 4.000 young Tartars have since then engaged in the service of the allied armies as labourers and carmen Scurvy, typhus and cholera have carried off at least the half ot the Tartars who had placed themselves under the immediate protection of the allies. Those who remain are generally of the class in better circumstances, and are consequently the most compromised. Russia will never forgive them, and feelings of humanity as well as of honour call on the allies to protect the inhabitants of a country whicIPhas just been subjected to invasion. The coasts of Anatolia are near, they are fertile and thinly peopled, and 20,000 Mussulman subjects the more would be for the Ottoman empire an element of riches more desirable and not less glorious than an extension of territory. It may be added that the Tartars, like all other oppressed races, surpass in activity, in intelligence, and in industry, the conquering party which for the last four centuries have reigned on the two shores of the Bosþÿphorus.

TIIE RUSSIANS AT KAltS The Russian journal Le Caucase contains intelligence of a late date from Kars. The greater number of the Imperial troops withdrew to the Russian territory when the hills and valleys of the conquered country became covered with snow. A brigade of the 18th division of infantry remains in garrison at Kars, and a detachment continues to occupy Ardaghan. The districts recently submitted to Russia are now tranquil, but an insurrection of a rather serious character broke out recently at Ghoel, situated to the North of Kars. It seems that Aslan Pacha and his brother Iser- Bek, assisted by a party of 400 men, incited the inhabitants to rise, and occupied the villages of Seinot Ivhorovanha and Tchoul-Penek. They were, however, unexpectedly attacked by three sotnias of Cossacks with four rocket batteries, and defeated. The insurgents (says Le Caucase) left sixty dead in the square of one of the villages, and four were taken prisoners. The Cossacks had of course, but one man killed and four wounded. WASHINGTON, Monday, Feb. 11 Mr. Dallas was in the Senate Chamber to-day, and looking remarkably well. He was courteously received by Senators of all parties. This appointment is believed to be very judicious, in every respect. It is said that Mr. Markoe, of the State Department, has been nominated as the Secretary of Legation, and that the nomination will be acted upon to-day. Despatches of some importance are expected from Mr. Buchanan by the Pacific. The reply of the British Government, if any be made, to our demand for Mr. þÿCrampton recall s and for the withdrawal ot Consuls Barclay, Matthew, Ac., may be expected. But whatever may have been the impression made by those specific demands on the British Government, and in whatever way they be noticed, it is not believed that it will lead to any disturbance of friendly relations with Great Britain. Mr. þÿDallas s instructions are in pro cess of preparation and he has had interviews with the President and Mr. Marcy. lie will, it is understood, depart very soon upon his mission. The condition of the fortifications of the harbor, and the Navy-yard, at New York, has been the subject of much remark, of late. They are utterly inadequate lor the purpose of defending the port, city, and Navy-yard, against the attack of such ships and armaments as are now afloat. A distinguished and scientific officer of the United States Navy remarked to Senators the other day, that lie would select two ships from the British Navy, with which he would undertake, with

perfect safety, to lay New York City under contribution, or shell and burn it. The officer knows the channel perfectly, and knows every gun that is or that can be mounted upon the forts on which we rely for the defence of the place. The guns of these forts are not of sufficient calibre and reach to do any harm to the class of ships which are now built by Great Britain. We are making some eleven inch guns ; but a proposition to arm the new steamer þÿ þÿMerrimack with them, was overruled by the Navy department. She is to be armed witli guns of much smaller calibre and range, and in contest with some modern English or French ships of war now afloat, she might as well lie armed with nothing but horse pistols. The exposed condition of New York has induced Senator Fish to offer a resolution of inquiry on the subject, which was adopted to day. Another fort at Sandy Hook for the purpose of preventing an þÿenemy s fleet from entering the outer harbor, has been spoken of as necessary. But the new, as well as the old forts, must, as is admitted, be equipped with entirely new armaments þÿ with guns of large calibre and long range. The Naval Committee of the Senate will soon report a bill in conformity with the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy, for budding twelve steam ships of war. There may be some opposition to it, on account of the prejudices existing against the present condition and management of the Navy, and the unpopularity of the action of the Naval Retiring Board.
I do not think, however, that the Committee on Naval Affairs will make

any preparation, either for the suspension of nominations already made, or for a revisionary Board, or for the restoration of officers who have been dropped or retired, or for a repeal of the law, pr any other ratibnal mode of relief. But it will be left with the President, at his discretion, to nominate to the Senate for vacancies which have occured, or may occur, such of the dropped or retired officers as he may please. That is the present state of opinion in the Committee on the subject. They may create a new naval corps, as the scientific corps, and thus Lieutenant Maury will be recognized as belonging to the Navy, and without being thrown out of his brevet rank, as he is now. The creation of such a corps would lie very useful to naval science.

A True Hero. þÿ On the night of the 31st Jan. the packet from Dover to Calais, after experiencing very heavy weather, was unable, in consequence of the continued violence of the storm, to enter the port of Calais. Two English travellers on board expressed great anxiety to catch the train for Paris, and insisted on being allowed to land. For this purpose they got into a small boat, with three sailors. The boat had scarcely left the þÿship side s when she was capsized by a tremendous sea, and the whole five were precipitated into the waves. An English gentleman, who had remained on deck, immediately took off his coat and sprang into the sea, and, at the imminent hazard of his own life, succeeded in reaching two of the unfortunate passengers, and brought them safely to the þÿship ladder. s He was himself assisted upon deck, little or none the worse þÿ the wetting excepted þÿ for his gallant exploit. On turning round he saw the other three persons struggling in the water, or holding on to the sides of the boat. Once more, in the coolest manner possible, he leaped into the sea, and succeeded, to the admiration ofall on board, in rescuing them. Thus the whole five were saved. The gentleman, with a modesty as rare as it was noble, refused to give his name, insisting that he had merely done his duty. The circumstances were made known in Calais in the morning ; and, when the passengers landed, the authorities of the town presented themselves to thank the hero of the adventure, and to demand his pass-

port. The passport, on being produced, bore the name of Lieutenant-General Sir Stephen Lakeman. The public will remember this gallant soldier in connection with the Kaffir War þÿ for his services in which he received the honour of knighthood. They will also remember his name in connection with the war on the Danube, and his successful maintenance of the rights of the Sultan in the Principalities, when he was Governor of the town of Bucharest. Sir Stephen holds the rank of Lieutenant-General in the service of the Sultan, under the title of Mazhar Pacha. We learn from Calais that the Societe de Secours Mutuel, of the Department of the Seine, a Society instituted for the Protection of Lives from Shipwreck, has just named him one of its Honorary Presidents, and forwarded him its gold medal, together with a diploma of membership, þÿ the latter bearing date the 15th of February. The true hero in war is the true hero in peace. All experience teaches this ; and the brilliant example of Sir Stephen Lakeman affords another and striking instance of it.

If it be objected that this plan entails more than ordinary trouble, I answer that it also ensures the safety of a valuable crop ; a consideration of no small importance. It must bo remembered that every seed will, under favorable conditions þÿ þÿtiller out so largely as to have from ten to twenty stalks or canes (as I shall henceforth call them), forming a large stool, and occupying a considerable space. I have found that rows three feet apart, with plants twelve inches from each other along the

I have had the þÿ N,ee-a þÿzana, in rows uuly two feet and again in rows two and a half feet apart, but I will not venture to say that in all cases such close planting is proper. The great objection to the adoption of close rows is the very serious one arising form the dif- 1 ficulty of cleaning and digging between them, I double that amount annually to the King of j which is so desirable, and so very conducive to their vigorous growth and perfect development þÿ for in common with almost all other plants, the Imphcc likes to have the soil loosened, and moved about around its roots. I suppose that it is almost unnecessary to observe that although Imphee likes abundance of moisture in the soil whereon it is growing, yet it has a decided objection to stagnant water being around its roots. As the plant progresses towards maturity it throws up its graceful flower, which very speedily is transformed into a seed head, most abundantly covered, or rather laden with grain. In the last chapter I alluded to the Kafir custom of removing these seed heads, shortly after

they appear, and 1 can only repeat the doubt I there expressed, whether by so doing we may not really lose more than we gain. When allowed to perfect its seed, the grain is generally plum and full of fine white flour, which I believe is wholesome and nutritious, aud might enter largely into general consumption. This in itself constitutes a feature, much iu favor of allowing it to ripen its seed þÿ and in a more general sense, is highly important. Notwithstanding my numerous unsuccessful attempts, some years ago, to impregnate, or fecundate the flowers of the sugar-cane, so as to obtain a seed which would germinate and produce sugar-canes, yet I cannot help clinging to this plant (Imphee) as the only remaining hope we now have of effecting this interesting object. I have already taken measures to have the new flowers of the sugar-cane brought into immense and continued contact with those of the Imphee, so as to ascertain for a certainty whether the sugar cane will thereby be induced to perfect its seed, and on the other hand, whether the pollen of the cane flowers will produce any beneficial or other chaugc iu the character of the Imphcc seed. This is a question of sufficient interest to engage the attention of every scientific aud enquiring mind, as it comprehends that which is interesting, and that which may be of great practical utility to the world at large. When the seeds of the Imphee are ripe, or perfectly full, it is the custom of the Zulu-kafirs to string them up in the sun and air for a few

days, then to hang them up in their buts, so that they may have the full benefit of the smoke, which serves to keep them entirely dry, and likewise preserves the seed from the attacks of insects, so that they may be thus kept perfectly good for a series of years if necessary I liked this plan so much that I adopted it in all its integrity, and can honestly recommend it toothers
