DENMARK The Sound Dues. þÿ It is said that the fresh proposals made by Denmark to the Sound Dues Congress consist in the offer to abolish them for

ever on the payment ot a sum of thirty-five millions of rix dollars, to be borne in fixed quotas by the Maritime States. The Councillor of State, Tengeborski, accepted this very moderate demand in the name of the Russian Government immediately and without any reserve, although Russia will have to bear nearly one-third of the whole sum. The Mecklenburg and Hanoverian Plenipotentiaries, who have all along supported Russia, also accepted the proposal, subject to the confirmation of their respective Governments, which there is no reason to doubt will be granted, as by that act they will be acknowledging the validity of þÿDenmark claims s to the Sound Dues, and probably calculate on a similar future recognition of their demand for the river dues at Baitzenburg on the Elbe, which bring in about 150,000 dollars to the Treasury at Schwerin, and the Stade Dues, which produce

Hanover. If the Danish proposals for capitalisation are generally accepted, it is intended to pay off with the proceeds the foreign debts of the kingdom contracted before the last war, including the English Three and Five per Cent Loans of 1825 and 1826; so that in future the whole of the national debt of Denmark will be confined to the loans contracted within the kingdom.

ENGLAND. IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS. OUR RELATIONS WITH AMERICA. On the motion for going into Committee of Supply, Mr. Roebuck moved, iu pursuance of the notice that lie had given, that an Address should be presented to the Crown praying for the production of all the correspondence that had lately passed between the Governments of England and the United States respecting the conduct of Mr. Crampton. The recent explanations given by Lord Palmerston respecting the apology offered to the States upon the enlistment question were, he said, inconsistent with certain facts which had come within his own cognisance Those facts Mr Roebuck then proceeded to detail, deriving his authority in great measure from the reports of some trials that had lately takeu place in America, and asserting as the result that Mr. Crampton had tried to evade the law and crimp the subjects of the United States Whether in these transactions the British Envoy had exceeded or followed his instructions from the Home Government, the Washington Cabinet were, he contended, equally entitled to insist upon his recall. Even when the alleged apology was made to the United States, the attempts at evading their law were not discontinued The object of his motion was on one hand to unmask the Government in what he considered a questionable proceeding, and on the other hand to afford Parliament an opportunity of repudiating all complicity in the transaction Mr. Hadfield seconded the motion. Lord Palmerston reiterated his previous state-

ment, that the correspondence in question was still in too incomplete a condition to be expediently made public. By tho last communication from the United þÿStates Government, the recall of Mr. Crampton was again demanded ; but a reply to that despatch could not be prepared until the Foreign Secretary had received an answer to the inquiries he had instituted respecting various statements on which this demand waa based. Ho deprecated discussion until all the papers were before the House, and declared that the Government had neither instructed nor desired Mr. Crampton to do anything that could possibly infringe the law of the country to which he was accredited In the course of the proceedings which furnished ground for the correspondence, Lord Palmerston asserted that several attempts had been made to entrap the British functionaries into illegal acts ; and he attributed those attempts to a conspiracy among certain individuals iu the States who desired to bring the two countries into collision. Denying, with much emphasis, that the apology offered to the States was cither insincere or insufficient, or that any evasion of their law had been practised, the noble Lord commented upon the dangerous nature of a discussion such as that Mr. Roebuck had challenged by his motion, and characterised the proceeding as unfair and unpatriotio. þÿ Mr. Disraeli could not support tho motion, whioh he considered premature in the absence of com plete and official information. þÿ The question
having been put, Mr. Roebuck declined to press bis amendment, and the original motion passed without a division

NOTICES OF NEW INVENTIONS. whitworth's improvements in firearms and projectiles. Until very recently the production of fire-arms has not participated in that general advance of mechanical art which distinguished most other departments of manufacture ; hut this state of things has now been very much changed, partly by the importation into this neglected field of mechanicians of Air. Whitworth's remarkable statements. Air. Whitworth lias taken out patents for his improvements. His latest improvements are a breech-loading apparatus, an improved projectile, and an improved method of boring and rifling the barrels of guns " 16 ratus consists of a heart-shaped piece of and cannon. The breech loading appametal, with two chambers, applied at the end of the barrel, and capable of vibrating on a pin situated at the lowest point of the heart. When pushed over to its furthest position in one direction one of the chambers containing the powder is brought opposite to the end of the barrel, and when pushed over to its lurthest position in the opposite direction the other chamber is brought opposite to the end of the barrel. One chamber is thus always opposite to the end of the gun, and the other projects sideways for reloading. Suitable arrangements are, of course, introduced for keeping up the metallic plate containing the chambers close against the end ol the barrel; and the hammer strikes upon t lie nipple of that chamber which is opposite to the end of t he gun. The new projectile is formed of a poly-

gonal and screw-formed shape, to suit the r:fling of the barrel, whereby a hard metal may he used for the formation of the projectile, and none of the force of the powder is lost in overcoming useless friction. Die improvements in I oring consist in the use of a tubular boring bar with longitudinal grooves on its circumference. The gun is bored in a vertical position, and the cutters enter at the bottom and travel upwards. The borings fill through the centre of the boring-bar, and the lubricating flunl is conducted to the cutters by the external grooves on the bar being forced up by a pump. To prevent the bar from springing it is kept in a state of tension by a suitable tensile strain applied at each end. In rifling it is, of course, necessary to combine the circular motion of the bar with a longitudinal motion; and, by a proper dividing apparatus being introduced, a light cut is taken out of each spiral groove all round the barrel, so that these grooves are all brought up alike, instead of each groove being finished before proceeding to the next. Fire-arms constructed according to Air. Whitworth's improvements will have an accuracy of firing hitherto unattaiued.

SEALING LETTERS. First close the envelope with a wafer, or adhesive gum ; then perforate it with a cross-cut common wafer seal, drop the melted sealing-wax on the perforated surface, and impress it with your usual seal. A letter so sealed cannot lie opened without entirely destroying the paper, as the agency of heat will not cause the gum or wafer to give way ; nor will moisture loosen the wax, which will hold through the orifices made by the wafer seal.

THE I M P H E E. To-day we were shewn a sample of ripe Cane from the Imphee seed, grown in this Island on the estate Windsor, the property of G. J. Mithe, Esquire ; also samples from a private gentleman of this town, of his own cultivation. We cannot venture to pronounce an opinion at present upon this cane, inasmuch as it has not yet been converted into sugar, neither has it had a fair trial in planting, &c. ; the samples we saw were productions of 2J and 3 months growth, and rather diminutive in size. The cane or sweet-reed of Imphee resembles more the Indian corn than the sugar-cane in appearance, although it appears to combine all the qualities of tinlatter. As we said before, its bulk is not equal to that of an ordinary size sugar-cane, but contains a proportionate quantity of saccharine matter. A great deal, however, in our opinion, depends upon the description of Itnphee þÿ as there are several varieties of it and the soil in which it is þÿ planted. " The Imphee delights and will grow famously, with sufficient moisture in rich alluvial soils, in good light brick mould, in loamy soils, and indeed in almost, every good soil in which there is an admixture of vegetable mould. Cleaning and digging around the plants are also desirable and very conducive to their vigorous growth and development." After the cane in question shall have undergone the processes of grinding and boiling we shall be glad to receive and publish a report of

(he quantity and quality of sugar it yields per acre of þÿland also the number of crops likely to be reaped each þÿyear, when only a fair estimate can be formed of it as a rival of the sugar-cane. Connected with the Imphee, we may state in conclusion, that " if after a season of long-continued showery weather a period of dry weather occurs, just as it ripens, then the juice is more especially abundant and rich in sugar."

THE WEATHER. Since our last report, on the weather no improvement has taken place. The dry weather has fairly set in, and the streets and roads are covered with dust ; the heat out-doors is insupportable ; and there is a general cry for rain ! Almost every cistern in town has been emptied, and we are without the prospects of an immediate supply of drinkable water. We fervently hope that in our next publication we may be enabled to speak more cheeringly on the season.

The latest arrivals from the United States bring before us their harassing question of slavery under an entirely and where new aspect, from which beams a warrantable hope that it will cease to be ere many generations have passed away. In referring to it, we shall neither east censure nor offer counsel ; we shall merely state facts, and leave our readers. both in England and America, to draw heir own conclusions. The subject, at all tunes delicate and irritating, is now likely to become of such intense interest that we cannot pass it hv in silence. Tile formation, a short time ag a I a ew territory, afterwards to bee oil derate state, has given oc active feud between the frc slave parties. In Kansas, as mis lei ntory is called, violent quarrels, bloodshed, and apprehended rebellion have lor weeks prevailed. The latest accounts state that collisions attended with bloodshed have occurred, that all parties are arming, and that a sanguinary intestine war is imminent. The tree party has formed companies, with numerous shareholders, and sent emigrants into Kansas as a profitable commercial and political speculation. The slave party has taken corresponding steps, and to secure the soil for slavery has seized political power. Slavery and freedom are thus brought face to face on the same spot, to contend for masterdoni. The people of the Southern states are fully convinced, as is stated in a recent number of The New Orleans Com-

3 S 0 I Z ATI 3 , mercial Bulletin, that the " growth of manufactures and the mechanic arts is a | remarkable feature in the towns of the North and East," and that "they do not increase in a similar manner in any part of the South." This is the testimony of the Southerns. For some time past, accordingly, they have taken great pains to introduce various kinds of manufactures into the South ; but even the manufacture of cotton, for which it might be supposed the Southerns have had some facilities, does not succeed. With a single exception, that of Granitevi lie, in South Carolina, all the numerous attempts have failed. The Southerns admit and say, " that the retrogression of many of the Southern states is to factures and other means of absorbing be traced directly to the want of manu- ' capital." The " same authority records instances Of thrifty planters and successful merchants looking to other lands for employment of the capital which years of assiduous labour and dashing enterprise have accumulated." They want to "invest their earnings in industrial enterprises of sure foundation, with and permanent returns. a moral certainty" ofobtaining " The absence profitable of such enterprises at the South, and the abundance of them at the North, has proved the strongest incitement to emigration to the North, and the transmission of capital." That no doubt may he left as to what is meant, a lamentafactures, instead of " being applied to Carolina is " invested in northern manu- tion follows that capital from South ."

drain the swamps, to resuscitate the worn-out lands, and to double the crops" of the parent state. Within twenty-five years it is estimated that a sum of twenty-five millions of dollars, accumulated in Charleston, has been carried off by its owners to contribute to the progressive prosperity of the " northern cities." To the cause of the South these are fatal admissions. Whatever theories may be adopted about " capital" þÿ the thing which all agree to call by that name is indispensable to improvement ; there is no accumulation of capital, and where capital cannot be profitably employed, there is no extension of enterprise, little or no improvements in the arts, and the condition of society approximates to stagnation or to " retrogression.'''' Whatever prejudices, too, may yet be nourished against " manufactures and the mechanic arts," it is certain that, unless they increase,

plain. Agriculture, as the rule, produces the necessaries of life þÿ manufactures and the mechanic arts the luxuries. 1 lie necessaries are gained by a small and diminishing quantity of' labour, as knowledge and skill are brought to hear upon agriculture, as instruments are improved, and as the principles on which feitility depends are better understood. There would, consequently he no employment for an increasing population þÿ no want of it þÿ no place for it in the world ; and it would not come into existence, or would not continue in existence, in " manufactures and the mechanic if it could not find employment arts." Even the agricultural slaves in the States would not increase in numbers if the growth of manufactures and the mechanic arts in the free states of America and in England did not provide a r ire and continually-increasing deal.. oil for their raw cotton. Without manufactures and without the mechanic arts, and without a continual improvement in both, prosperity aid progress

are impossible. Manufactures are not merely advantage an to a few capitalists, but are essential to the well being of society. They do not flourish in the slave states of America, they flourish amazingly in the free states. They have been brought to their present condition and are continually improved by discoveries in chemistry, electricity, meteorology, pneumatics, hydraulics, by discoveries concerning heat, light, friction, &c. Now, in the South, in consequence of slavery, the bulk of the population is doomed designedly to ignorance. In the North, as a consequence of freedom, the whole population is carefully in structed. Experience has taught us that knowledge or mind working by the help of nature is real power; and every free man in the North, considered as a productive agent, is an intellectual giant. He is equal to any slave-owner, while all the slaves are utter pigmies and dwarfs compared to him. They invent no machinery, they make no discoveries, they can scarcely use machinery when invented, or profit by discoveries when made by free men. They do both only to a small extent. It is reasonable to suppose, therefore, that but for the neighbourhood of freedom, which sheds some of its radiance over slavery, the slave states of the South would fall back to the level of the kingdom of Dahomey. Increase of knowledge is always in proportion to the number of minds free to observe, inquire, investigate, and give expression to thought ; and in a society composed of forty-nine

slaves and one master the intellect of only the fiftieth portion is developed. Such a society can of itself make no progress in knowledge or in power. All the energies of the intellectual small minority employed in supporting the are system of constraint. Thus slavery dooms the South to comparative ignorance, to comparatively slow progress ; or, even as some advocates of slavery admit, to retrogression. On a future occasion we shall have some further facts to communicate upon this part of the subject. In the mean time we commend those on which we have already commented to the serious consideration of all the opponents of slavery, and of all who look with interest and favour on the growth and prosperity of the United States.

Count Ficquelmont, who cannot for give or forget that the British Government in 1848 and 1849 was willing to deprive Austria of a part of her Italian possessions, has just published a work on the Eastern question, which contains a great deal of abuse of the policy of England, and one or two facts worth notice. The Count, who not long be fore the Hungarian revolution had been Austrian Minister at St. Petersburg, relates that in 1840 the Russian Government recognised the principle of the freedom of the Danube, and formally pledged itself to keep in such a state " that there should the Sulina arm always be water enough for merchantmen." After the convention between Russia and Austria had been signed, and the ratifications exchanged, the St. Petersburg Government ordered the naval authorities at Odessa to see that the sand did not accumulate at the entrance to the Sulina, and they for a time obeyed the instructions which had been given them. The importance of the Danube to Austria and Southern G rrnany was at once seen, and the traffic increased so rapidly that Galatz speedily became a place of importance, and the greater mart for the agricultural produce of the Danubian Principalities. As soon as the Odessa authorities remarked that Galatz was likely to become a formidable rival, they neglected to remove the sand from the embouchure of the Sulina arm, and the navigation of the Danube was interrupted. As soon as it was evident that ihe larger vessels could not pa s the bar, a company of specula-

tive Greeks appeared with a little flotilla of li.'liters, and demanded and received such enormous prices for their services, " that tin y could afford to allow a certain salary to Ihe Russian employes for their inactivity." Such was the state of things ten years ago, and such it is even now.

THE COLONIAL COUNCIL. From a trust-worthy source we learn that the Colonial Council will be convoked in the course of this month. Of the only two remaining representatives of St. Thomas, viz. Messrs. A. H. Ruse and J. Cappe, the former has recently resigned his seat on account of a voyage to Europe. A new election, therefore, at all events to fill up one vacancy, will be requisite. This fact has enabled Government once more to grant to the Electors of St. Thomas an opportunity of effecting the due and proper representation of their community, inasmuch as it is intended, by such election, to fill all the 5 vacant seats. We cannot doubt for a moment, notwithstanding all the indifference hitherto manifested, that the electors of St. Thomas will listen, this time, to the summons ; that they will meet at the poll and give their votes in favor of persons who, they feel assured, will accept the task imposed upon them. For it can hardly be unknown to them, that among other matters which, in the course of the impending session of the Colonial Council, will be laid before it, there are several that must most materially affect the future welfare of the Island of St. Thomas. We allude to the question of procuring the necessary funds, in order

to clear the harbor of mud and to blast the rocks discovered in it ; undertakings which, as tar as we can learn, will require a capital of $146,000, besides the expenses connected with the eventual building of a stone-quay along the sea-lots, þÿ as also the establishment of a quarantine hospital on Buck Island, &c. It may, perhaps, be said that all these matters more nearly regard the Royal, and not the Land Treasury ; the electors of St. Thomas ought, however, to bear in mind that, even setting aside the question whether or not their community will of said expenses, eventually have to in take over every case at least a part the Colonial Council will have to report to His Majesty the King on the Revenues and Expenses of the Royal Treasury in these Islands ; but that, if that one specific Island, on account of which the State Treasury is expected and required to incur such heavy expenses, will persist in showing so little interest for the institution in question, as not even to cause representatives to meet and render their opinions on the exigencies of the Island, it can assuredly be expected neither that the representatives of the other Islands should evince any great zeal in forwarding the special interests of St. Thomas, nor, should even an honorable and strict sense of duty impel them to do so, that their opinion in this direction would have the same weight with the King and the Diet of the Mother-Country, which it unquestionably would have if proceeding from those who are most loudly called on

to stand forward in their own interests. However, we repeat, we cannot suppose otherwise than that the Electors of St. Thomas will feel the necessity of having their Island duly represented in the Colonial Council.

ASTRONOMICAL DISCOVERY rer I lie New York " Courier and observes, in transferring to its Enquicolumns the notice of the following recent discovery in Astronomical science, that the credit of the discovery is due to Prof. Pierce of Harvard College: advocacy of that The the universally moon is uninhabited, because accredited theory, she has no atmosphere, has received, from a recent discovery, a blow that will unsettle it at least. That the moon, as tar as we have yet been able to excorrespondent of the Globe says : þÿ amine her, has no atmosphere, or at form least none of sufficient density to con- to our optical laws, and the demands of any animal life known to us, is unquestionable. But this can be positively affirmed of only one side of our satellite ; for, as will be remembered, although she revolves upon her axis, she constantly presents hut one side to the earth. Now it has been discovered by calculation, and demonstrated as geometrical fact, that the moon's centre of form is eight miles nearer to us than her centre of gravity, through which, of course, her axis of revolution must pass ; or, in other words, this side of the moon is sixteen miles higher than the other. If, therefore, we suppose that the moon has an atmosphere such as ours, it would he of such extreme rarity on the only side exposed to our observation, that, for optical effect and animal life, it might as well not exist. For mountains upon the earth, none of which are over five miles above the level of the sea,
have been ascended to a height at which life could not he supported for any

stretched above the panting traveller. What, then, must be the atmosphere at four times such an elevation? The conclusion seems inevitable, that, although the hither side of the moon is uninhabitable for want of an atmosphere, the remote side may be perfectly adapted to animal life. It is at least certain that the mere want of an atmosphere perceptible to us is no longer conclusive as to the uninhabitableness of the planet that rules the night. We announce this discovery on the authority of one of the most eminent mathematicians and astronomers in the world. It will soon be formally declared in a scientific quarter.

The St. Thomas « Tidende," of the 16th instant, reports that, a very ingenious theft had been committed at that Island on the night of the 1 2th, by the abstraction front the glass case in the store of Messrs. A. & P. Gellibert, of Jewellery amounting in value to about 81,000. It is supposed that the thief must have secreted himself in the store before the closing of the doors. We agree with our ' contemporary that the act exhibits a good deal of daring, in as much as the store is small, and the chances of concealment before closing more hazardous." Let us hope that the guilty party may so " reap the fruit of his labour" as to deter others from doing likewise.

i I he "Tidende" (of St. Thomas) furni-hes intelligence from Sto. Domingo of a later date than we were in receipt þÿof wherein we find that another battle had been fought between the Dominicans and the Haytieus, in which the latter were totally vanquished. " This battle, which was fought in the North, completes the defeat of the Haytiens both North and South, and we must believe totally defeats any future attempt, on their part, of organising an army from the remnants of the two now beaten, and so thoroughly demoralised as doubtless to defy their being brought together again. No doubt this fight will put an end to the war ; and the Emperor Soulouque, if he can escape a civil war, which is much doubted, will probably learn wisdom from bis present folly, and seek by means of internal improvement to produce prosperity and contentment in his realm, and, as a previous step thereto, grant a general amnesty to those who are in expatriation from their native land." The terms are said to be that Spain shall furnish an array of from ten to twenty thousand men for the Eastern war, and receive from England and France protection of her interests in Cuba. If this story is true þÿ and I am inclined to credit it þÿ it affords an evidence that the augmented fleets of the Allies, and the Spanish fleet expected to rendezvous in the neighbourhood of San Juan, look to the protection of Cuba rather than an interference in Central American affairs. " Lord Palmerston, doubtless, is very glad to avail bimself of this opportunity to create the impression that the American interpretation of the Clayton-Bulwer treaty is to be disputed by force, with the hope, perhaps, of frightening us out of what we believe to be just and right. If such is his expectation, he will be mistaken ; for, so far as I can judge, public sentiment is unanimously in favor of the most unyielding resistance to Palmerston's pretentions. I say Palmerston, because I do not believe the English people will ever sustain him." " Washington, Jan. 23. þÿ I perceive that

some of the papers persist in asserting the imminence of a war with Great Britain. This is the way to bring one on if it is desired. There is nothing in any of the questions between the i United States and Great Britain deemed by any of our statesmen here at all dangerous to our peace, if the country only stands up boldly for the right, instead of inviting persistence in foreign aggression by seeming to be afraid of it. True, we have the statement that Mr. Cushing has declared that war would exist between England and the United States ; but I have no hesitation in assuming that ho has said nothing of the sort, for I know such a declaration to be directly the reverse of his views, as frequently expressed in conversation." Boston, February 1. þÿ The Cunard steamship Arabia, Captain Stone, has arrived here from Liverpool with the mails, thenee of Saturday, the 19th ult., comprising intelligence from Great Britain and from Europe generally one week later than that received by the Baltic. Her news is calculated to excite much interest. Consols are reported to have been active with prices closing at 89 at latest quotations. In coffee, prices arc also reported to have had an upward tendency

THE PEACE NEGOTIATIONS. VIENNA, Wednesday. The Ost- Deutsche Fast states that Austria will forthwith propose to the German Diet to adhere to the peace prelinimaries, in order that representatives ot Germany proaching conferences.

A RATIONAL MEW OF THE WAR (From the X. Y. Journal of Commerce, Dec. 24.) The important question presented in the papers brought by the Asia regards the probability of an immediate peace. Tbe point upon which, in our view, the question turns is this, þÿ whether Russia has been, and will be, more benefitted than damaged by a continuation of the war ? It is very evident from the results of this þÿyear s campaign, that the power of Russia in war has been greatly exaggerated. landed in the Crimea on the 14th of September, 1854. They have occupied it now for more than si year, and, instead of being expelled by startling a exhibition of force, the allied Powers, after a tedious and sanguinary struggle, have obtained command over the port of Sebastopol, a fortress built up by Russia to enable her to carry out her vast schemes of southern territorial aggrandisement, þÿ have destroyed not only its buildings, docks, arsenals, and fortifications, but also the fleet which issued from it to strike terror into every seaport in the Black Sea. The destruction has been so complete that it is stated that not a piece of wood six inches in length can now be found within its limits. Kinburn, which commanded the north of the Dnieper þÿ of the utmost consequence to South Western Russia þÿ was assaulted by the allied forces in the middle of October, was taken, and is quietly held, greatly to the annoyance of the trade of the empire Omar Pasha is now engaging the Russian forces within her Transcaucasian possessions ; is endeavouring, bv the

strickest observance of every private right, to win over the variable inhabitants to his cause ; and has already accomplished such important results by force of arms as seriously to threaten the power of Russia in that important theatre ot her operations. Parts of Georgia and Circassia have throughout refused to declare allegiance to the Czar, and other portions which yielded from a mistaken belief in the omnipotence ot Russia, more than from desiro, may be induced to quit the army of the empire, and ally themselves to these whose policy must, necessarily give them the benefits of freedom and intercourse with mankind. Odessa, the groat port of Southern Russia, is damaged and further threatened ; the Don, which after connecting itself hv means of a

canal with the mighty V'olga and the Caspian, j commanded by the allies ; and discharged itself into the Sea of the Azofl, is also Baltic has been shut up from the very commencement of the war. To a power which sent its armies into the Danubian provinces for purposes of conquest this is a mortifying exhibition. It shows that Russia, withdrawn into her vast shell, relies on her capacity for endurance and resistance, than upon her active and manly displays of courage and power outside of her dominions. The pride and spirit of the people, without which no nation can be invincible, must sink low under this display. Their assailants, animated with success, and feeling the justice of their cause, are strengthened and encouraged in the ratio in which Russia is depressed. But what does the next year forebode to the fortunes of the Czar, if peace should not be reached ? The alliance with Sweden assures Alexander that the idea of Russian omnipotence þÿ that valuable inheritance of a nation þÿ is fast dwindling away ; and it intimates that Austria and other States, which have hitherto wavered between their wishes and their fears, may aid in crippling a power which hitherto has advanced with sure steps around the Euxine, uuder a prestige of manifest destiny that none could dispute. If Sweden should join the allies, the fall of St. Petersburg will be almost certain, and the Moss of Swedish Finland probable. Russia has has been a bold and unscruplous robber on every side of her dominions. Sweden,

Poland, Turkey, and Persia have each been despoiled of valuable possessions to extend the limits of Russian empire, and they know full well the policy as to the future which the past proclaims. The papers in the interest of the Czar ( there are none others within its limits) tell us that preparations are going forwards on an immense scale, and that the war will be prosecuted with vigour. A new levy of 10 men out of every 1,000 has beeu ordered, caused, the telegraph from Berlin states, by the dread that Sweden and Denmark arc about to join the Western alliance. The levy, it says, þÿ has already begun ; may he admitted to the ap- I vinces will, it is thought, prevent its producing but the season and the exhaustion of the proi the force calculated þÿon. If there had been a j force within the limits of Russia competent to | give adequate protection to St. Petersburg it would have been sent to Sebastopol, that one of the ancient objects of Russian diplomacy and arms might not be frustrated by its capture þÿ the extention of Russia along the Dardenelles and Bosphorus to the Mediterranean, and perhaps | by the Euphrates to the Gulf of Persia. The failure to protect Sebastopol is a confession of weakness, which the boasts of Russia through her journals cannot efface. The future must be announced to Russia in the past. She has to choose either the disgrace of peace, or the dis- The allied forces j grace and damage of successive defeats. The papers tell us that there are no proposi-

tions for peace from Russia. There are suggestions, however, from Austria, and an ominous change in the tone of the press in France, which must have an important origin. Canrobert arrived at Paris on the 3d December. There were intimations that his mission had been successful. His visit to Stockholm had for its object the most vigorous prosecution of the war He was received by the King with every demonstration of respect, and the probability of an alliance having been formed is very great. Tbe threats to Russia which such an alliance would involve, in connexion with the disasters to her which have marked the þÿyear scampaign, are calculated to produce suggestions to the allies, or at least to France, of a peaceful character, such as would lead the Emperor to prepare the nation for their accept ance. Those papers which hitherto have been warlike have suddenly urged the importance of peace to the national interest of the French. If the mission to Stockholm had failed it would scarcely have boon prudent, flushed although France is with the honours of the recent and great victories, to urge the necessity of peare immediately on the return of the French Ambassador, inasmuch as the failure of Canrobert would have produced a necessity for extending the warlike feeling in France to a still higher pitch The chances of peace would seem therefore to be strengthened by recent events ; but snob is the hereditary obstinacy of Russia þÿ such the danger to the Government of abandoning a fa-

vourite policy to which the mind of the nation has been directed by all her þÿSovereigns such the impracticability of her rulers, and so powerful the influence of passion, acting under disappointment and mortified þÿpride that it would not he sale to predict a speedy return of peace.

Latest Intelligence ! BERLIN, Thursday. It is understood that a mere protocol acknowledging the willingness of the belligerent Powers to treat on the conditions proposed is all that will be signed

at Vienna. The formal preliminaries of peace will not he signed till the represent Jives of the various Powers meet at Paris. Neither Sardinia nor Prussia will be parties to the protocol. Both will be admitted to the after negotiations. We (Times) have received the follow ing telegraphic dispatch from our Veinna correspondent : þÿ VIENNA, Thursday, Jan. 31, 10 a m, The Turkish Embassy in this city has been empowered to sign the Protocol if necessary. THE BALTIC. We have received intelligence here that the Russians have taken advantage of the late temporary thaw to sink immense blocks of stone at the entrance of the Isle of Nargen. Care will be taken before the navigation reopens to render the ground utterly impracticable as an anchorage for ships of the line. The accounts we receive of the commercial activity in the Gulfs of Bothnia and Finland, since there has been a prospect of peace, are almost incredible. PREPARATIONS FOR THE NEXT CAMPAIGN. TRIESTE, Thursday. Accounts from Constantinople of the 21st state that, in spite of the pacific news, General Shirley has sent orders to Schumla to prepare quarters for the troops that are to proceed there in the spring. Ministerial changes are considered imminent at Constantinople. Mehemet Ali will, it is said, he named Minister of War.

THE EMPEROR ALEXANDER II. The Continental journals publish a variety of statements, interesting as being assumed to display the disposition and þÿcharac er of the Russian Emperor. The Constitutionnel says that on the 16th, when the acceptance of the Austrian propositions was declared, the Emperor called none of the chief men ot tinempire to his council, sent for no one, except Count de Nesselrode, M. de Seniawine and M. de Fonton, and for them only to make known his irrevocable decision, and to order them to transmit it to Veinna and to Count Valentine Esterhazy. There was no advice and no discussion. The sovereign gave the order ; the great dignitaries of his empire obeyed, and that was all they had to do. The members of the Imperial family knew nothing of the affair before tin- La þÿPlata personages just mentioned. One alone, the Empress Maria, knew beforehand the decision of her august consort, since it was owing, in a great measure to her influence that the decision was come to. In addition to the recommendations ot' her Majesty, Prince Gortschakoff was constantly sending dispatches of the most alarming character, and which invariably terminated with such phrases as this: þÿ þÿ foresee I the most serious complications for us if we continue the war; I entreat your Majesty to adhere to the conditions proposed ; the whole ol Europe declares against þÿRussia The Constitutionnel is also informed that the Emperor Alexander addressed i a most friendly letter to the Emperor of Austria on the existing negotiations,

and expressing a decided wish for the early re-establishment of peace. It is said that the Emperor Alexander has expressed the desire that the content of his letter should he communicated to the Emperor Napoleon. This communication having taken place, the

Emperor of the French a is said to have addressed, in his turn, very friendly letter to the Emperor Francis Joseph, and it is added that the latter has communicated it to the Court of St. Peters burg.

FRANCE. The Constitutionnel gives the important intelligence that the signature of the preliminaries of peace is reserved for the Congress (for so with more or less accuracy the coming Conference is now termed). The armistice, which will be the þÿ natural and immediate þÿconsequence of the signature, will not, of course, according to the hypothesis, take place till after the Congress meets and with respect to the period, the Constitutionnel, admitting that it is difficult to make any exact calculation, thinks the deliberations cannot begin earlier than from the 20th to the 25th of February. Meanwhile, the public mind in Paris is so completely made up to consider peace as good as signed, that no attention is paid to suggestions of possible difficulties, or to details of any kind.

THE OVERLAND RAIL. INDIA. We have received our files of papers by the Overland Mail, via Trieste. The following brief summary of political intelligence is extracted from the Bombay Times of Jau. 2 : þÿ þÿ The Santal insurrection may be said to be suppressed. Tranquillity prevails throughout our dominions, and we have not for some months had a single disturbance, even on the Punjab frontier. The kingdom of Oude is about to be sequestered, the King to be allowed £100,000 a year, the army to bo reduced from 80,000 to 15,000 ; the entire administration of affairs to be entrusted to the Resident General Outram. The settlement of the Odeypore differences, which renders the political agent supreme, has dissatisfied the chiefs. The native Princes, whose administration is admitted to be blameless, are endeavouring to obtain some better security | than they have hitherto enjoyed for the retention of their dominions

From the Illustrated London News, Jan. 19. It is stated, evidently upon some kind of authority, aud in order that the subject may be fully discussed as soon as Parliament meets, that the disastrous fall of Kars may in great measure be attributed to the personal hostility of our Ambassador at Constantinople towards General Williams. It is alleged that Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, who has a talent for hating, manifested this hostility as soon as General Williams began to show evidence of talent of another and more valuable kind, and that Lord Stratford had unhappily the means of rendering himself mischievous, by inducing the Turkish Government to withhold the assistance so urgently needed : and the want of which, if it have not disgraced our arms, has imperilled the fortunes of a campaign, and rendered peace more difficult to conquer and to maintain. Sixty-three despatches to Lord Stratford were, it is stated, sent by the sorelypressed but heroic General. They all remained without reply. When ultimately, the Ambassador was forced, by orders from home, to attend to General þÿWilliam communications, s it was too late to prevent the melancholy catastrophe. Lord Stratford has rendered great services to his country in former years ; he has played a conspicuous and beneficial part in all the transactions immediately prior to the declaration of war against Russia ; and is a diplomatist of such consummate ability that Great Britain would be much the bet-

3 'J » 8 m 4 a 2L A -T i 3. ter for half a dozen like him. Of the peculiarities of his þÿLordship s character the public have hardly to be informed, especially since the þÿ Roving þÿEnglishman let in a little coloured light upon them ; but we should reluctantly believe that he had been guilty of conduct for which, if it be proved, there is no punishment in the statute-book to severe. In fact, if the charge be true, and Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, from private malice, has neglected his duty to his þÿQueen ally, s he is a traitor. There is no use in mincing words. We sincerely hope that, for the honour of England, the veteran Ambassador may be able to clear himself before his Peers ; for those who make the attack cannot stop short of impeachment.

SUSPENSION OF HOSTILITIES BY RUSSIA. The following statement, which appeared in the Morning Post of Wednesday, is contradicted by the Paris correspondent of the Times, who says, It would be contrary to all diplomatic þÿ usage to issue such orders before the preliminaries of peace have been signed þÿ : þÿ We believe that authentic intelligence has been received from St. Petersburg that, on the 18th inst., the Emperor dispatched an order to the Russian Generals in the Crimea to suspend hostilities. This important public step argues the sincerity of þÿRussia desire s for peace þÿ a desire which wo hope may soon be gratified on complete and suf- I ficient conditions. At the same time, it is only right to observe that the acceptance by Russia of the Austrian ultimatum does not justify us in yet suspending hostilities. We must ourselves sign preliminaries of peace before we can abstain from acts of war. It is also but fair to remark that, at the present season of the year, an order to suspend hostilities, where none can go forward, ! amounts to a mere formality. As such, however, I it is indicative of the anxiety which no doubt exists at St. Petersburg to commit us to a pacific course. We cannot, however, forget that all that is now peaceful in the aspect of affairs is purely due to our past successes and our present preparations, and that, if we would be sure of peace, our wisest and safest course is to continue our active exertions until we sign with Russia the preliminaries of a treaty þÿ a step which will,

! pro facto, be succeeded by a cessation of bostili- I ties. So far as this country is concerned, it is satisfactory to know that the warlike preparations in our dockyards and factories arc going forward with undiminished briskness. The Globe, which has the best opportunity of knowing, speaks very strongly on this point : þÿ Gun-boats are being completed and commissioned, mortars are being cast, recruits come in increased numbers in consequence of Lord þÿPanmure re- s cent change in the bounty, drill and rifle practice are carried on with assiduity, stores arc being shipped offþÿ all with an energy unsurpassed at any period of the war. As an indication that our preparations arc not decreased in point of extent, we may mention that within the last few hours a requisition has been sent for transport accommodation for 4000 horses þÿ nearly 60,000 tons of shipping. General þÿCodrington s army, according to the latest accounts, numbered more than 54,000 men, in admirable condition and spirits, and were fast approaching the highest discipline. Some of the regiments, we hear, present a picture surpassing the most brilliant display of infantry movements that Hydc-park has witnessed for several years. This training and preparation for a campaign will go on until

we know absolutely that there will be no campaign. It is not necessarily to be argued from all this that the Government distrusts the desire of Russia to come to terms in the interest of European security. A knowledge of her internal circumstances would perhaps suggest a different presumption. But Lord Palmerston has the honour of England in his keeping, and while meeting cordially the advances to peace, he will carefully provide for a possible failure of diplomacy, by bringing into full working order that machinery which, in conjunction with the arms of our allies, has hitherto been so instrumental in achieving success.

The Proposed Campaign or 1856. þÿ The Paris correspondent of Lt Nord says that the following obtains belief in diplomatic circles in that city : þÿ þÿ Baron de Seebach informed Count Nesselrode that, if the negotiations failed to establish peace, the plan of campaign for this year would consist in making Austria and Prussia cede Gallicia and the Duchy of Posen in order to reconstitute the kingdom of Poland; an Austrian Archduke would become independent Sovereign of Poland, and a land force would operate in Finland. The English would engage to take Cronstadt. The Principalities would be ceded to Austria, with the frontiers pushed back in Bessarabia as far as the line of mountains fixed in the first of the four propositions. Finally, the Prussian ports would be strictly blockaded þÿ

The Council of War. þÿ The Council of War assembles daily at Paris, under the presidency of the Emperor ; but the strictest secrecy is maintained respecting the deliberations. The Debats of Tuesday says that one of the principal questions under discussion is the unity of the command of the Allied armies. The Paris correspondent of the Independav.ee Beige believes that the campaign will be continued in the Crimea, and that the expedition to the Baltic, to be almost exclusively English, will be without an army for disembarkation. The same writer mentions a report that the new French loan þÿ will be subscribed, if not entirely in England, at least with a solidarity of the resources of the two nations, and guaranteed by the two Governments þÿ

GEMS OF THOUGHT. He that would have fine guests, let him have a fine wife. Religion is the best armor in the world, but the worst cloak. He that hath a trade, hath an estate ; and he that hath a calling, hath a place of profit and honor. A ploughman on his legs is higher than a gentleman on his knees. When the idea of any pleasure strikes your imagination, make a just computation between the duration of the pleasure, and that of the repentance that is likely to follow it. Nothing can we call our own, but death ; and that small model of the barren earth (the grave), which serves as paste and cover to our bones. The talent of turning men into ridicule, and exposing to laughter those one converses with, is the gratification of little minds and ungenerous tempers. A young man with this cast of mind, cuts himseli off from all manner of improvement. Gentility is neither in birth, wealth, manner, nor fashion þÿ but. in the mind. A high sense of honor, a determination never to take a mean advantage of another, an adherence to truth, delicacy and politeness towards those with whom we have dealings, are its essential characteristics.

Hints about Halls. þÿGentlemen sDress. þÿ Your dress should be a black coat by one of the first tailors (dress coat) ; a white silk rolled coller vest ; linen frilled and superbly white, cuff seen ; black tights if you are well made ; if not, trowsers half tight and neat ; black silk Lyons stockings ; a handsome black silk stock, having a neat bow; a very fine cambric handker chief, plain border, slightly perfumed ; brequet in vest, and slight chain, white kid French gloves, exactly fitting the hand ; the cliaussure insurpassably neat and luisante. Never go to a public hall before a late hour. Dance no more than four sets with one lady under any pretence. You may converse with your partner, soto voce but only furtively with any other lady while standing up in the dance. You cannot be too attentive to your partner, nor must you leave her while engaged to dance with her ; you must either stand or sit near her. Rules for Ladies at Halls. However rich the materials for your dress may be, let it be remarkable for simplicity, and let the hair he as little decorated as possible. Avoid affectation, frowning, quizzing, or the slightest indication of ill-temper. Create not the heart burnings of jealousy, by forgetting a lover, for some face in a ball-room. Your handkerchief should be as fine as a þÿ snowy þÿcobweb, it should he bordered with deep rich lace and delicately perfumed. Gloves (French,) white kid ; shoes small, waferlike andfitting exquisitely. French silk stockings. You are permitted to com-
mand the most unlimited services of your partner, but should impose this task upon him in such a manner as to make it delightful

OUR RELATIONS WITH AMERICA. Some people, not usually deficient in worldly

ignorant of the causes of the war against Russia. The old proverb that there are none so blind þÿ as those who will not þÿsee sufficiently explains their state of mind. But this class of persons þÿ of whom Mr. Bright may be considered the leader and spokesman þÿ docs not suffer from the same infirmity of temper in the case of the untoward quarrel which has sprung up betwixt this country and the United States. They know all about it, and share the opinions of their countrymen þÿ that a war, if it unfortunately arise, will not bo one of

þÿEngland seeking s ; and that the guilt and shame of it will be upon the heads of those officials in the United States who do everything to provoke and nothing to prevent it. The causes of difference are so simple that all the world can appreciate them. Great Britain is accused by a party in the interest of the actual President, and by the principal law-officer of that great magistrate, of an infraction of the laws of the United States, in having encouraged, through the agency of the British Minister at Washington, the enlistment of American citizens for the British Foreign Legion. The British Government did not seek to defend its ill-advised and useless act. It ceased the enlistment immediately that complaint was made, aud offered an apology more than sufficient to satisfy the greatest of European Powers which might, under similar circumstances, have felt itself aggrieved. If Great Britain and the United States could have been personified as two honest, sensible, high-minded, chivalrous, Christian gentleman, the apology tendered by this country would not only have been deemed sufficient, but would have strengthened between the two, the friendship that had b.'on threatened with interruption. The plaintiff" in the cause would have felt esteem as well as admiration for the ready courtesy and manly bearing of the defendant ; and would have confessed in his secret heart that one who could afford to be so just was a friend worth having May not this yet be the turn which events will

take on the other side of the Atlantic ? We sin- La þÿPlata cerely trust that it will. Even Mr. Bright, whom the prospects of peace with Russia have inclined to be reasonable, takes pains to declare before the Manchester Chamber of Commerce, world, that on this question he is þÿ as much against doing anything that could bring humiliation on his country as any man can Tuesday , þÿbe. But President Pierce, and those who share with him the honours and emoluments of office,

this country. We do not believe that this gentlemau and his party truly represent the feeling of the United States in this matter. Whether they do, or not, Great Britain will not inflict humiliation upon herself to please his vanity, or to further his supposed interests, or the necessities of his ambition. Strong in the consciousness both of Might aud of Right, this nation may afford to forgive an insult wantonly inflicted ; but it will not inflict degradation upon itself by dishonourable and pusillanimous acquiescence in demands that ought never to have been made. If the Government of Mr. Pierce have determined not to tolerate the presence of Mr Crampton as Representative in Washington, so be it. Let Mr. Pierce request that Minister, if ho pleases, to pack up his goods and chattels and return to London ; and it is highly probable that this country will be magnanimous enough to forgive the discourtesy, and to endeavour to find consolation for the want of a representative at the White House. The heavens will not crack ; the sun will not cease to shine, or the earth to yield its harvests, because there is þÿ an Excelþÿlency the less on the other side of the Atlantic, or because Mr. Pierce has behaved in his public capacity in a manner which in his private capa. city as a gentleman he would neither have imitated nor recommended. The other cause of dispute þÿ that relative to the worthless islands of Belize, quite as simple, is and of as little importance to this country. A

gentleman, if we appeal to his generosity, will often give away a thousand pounds, and be glad of the opportunity, but he will not be bullied out of a farthing. Whether, under the Clayton- Bulwer treaty, these islands ought or ought not to be considered under the protectorate of Great

Britain, is not of the slightest consequence to this nation, except in so far as a groat principle is concerned. The British Government has offered to submit the case to arbitration, and to abide by the award. What more can honest America desire ? There is not a man in these islands who would not rather give the United States the town and dependencies of Belize þÿ were they a thousand times more valuable than they þÿare than waste a pound of powder or singe the hair of an þÿEnglishman or s þÿAmerican head s in the quarrel to retain them. If the þÿ bumptiþÿous Mr. Pierce will not submit to arbitration, he is condemned beforehand in the great tribunal of civilisation ; and forces the sympathy and the conscience of the world to declare themselves ; self to pay at some future day. She against him. We hare no fear, as some of our contemporaries have, of wounding what is called the þÿ susþÿceptibility of the United States. It is enough that this nation should apologise for an unintentional wrong ; and submit its real or assumed rights to the arbitration of any State or Sovereign that the Americans themselves will name ; hut that Englishmen should speak with þÿ bated þÿbreath, lest their too-jealous and thin-skinned cousins should take offence, is too much. This country is not afraid of America ; and will not

Englishmen will speak their mind on this question as on every other. Their mind is that a war with the United States would be a most deplorable þÿcalamity a scandal to our blood, our civilisation, and our religion þÿ a horror too great to be adequately þÿdesignated and a catastrophe that they would do anything to avoid consistent with the honour which makes the character of nations as well as of individuals. If misjudging or passionate men in America shall force us into such a war þÿ in spite of warning þÿ in spite of þÿapology in spite of justice þÿ; on their heads will be the penalty aud the shame. Great Britain, washing her hands of the guilt and the responsibility, will go into the struggle with a sorrowful but a resolute heart ; and it will be strange indeed if America do not get the worst of it.

It is expected that in a fortnight from this day (Feb. 9) the Conferences of Paris will be formally opened. If the adhesion of Russia to the terms proposed by Austria, and approved by Great Britain and France, be as þÿ pure and þÿsimple as represented, the work to be performed by this illustrious assembly will be þÿ þÿsimple also. Yet wc cannot but suspect, however complete may be the agreement between the European Powers as to the Four Points which relate more particularly to the Turkish part of the question, that long debates, it not differences, will arise on the vague Fifth Point. That point may include stipulations to which Russia may not feel bound to accede It has been purposlye left elastic ; and may comprise more or less, as Russia shows herself to be more or sincerely desirous to keep the peace of Europe. The treaty concluded between Great Britain and France on the one side, aud Sweden and .Norway on the other, binds the Allies to insist that Bomarsund shall never be rebuilt as fortress or arsenal, þÿ in either of which characters it could serve no purposes but those of aggression. Russia had no necessity for such an arsenal, in such a position ; and if she insist upon rebuilding it, or forming any other within the same proximity to Sweden, the Allies will be justified in interpreting her desire in a sense adverse to the independence of Sweden, and as a menace to Europe, The Allies, appears, it have tacitly, perhaps more or authoritatively, allowed Russia to understand
that no demand will be made upon her for the

3 if. 0 It b J a; at a s expenses to which she has put them in resisting her unjust aggression ; but, if such nations as Great Britain and France can afford to be generous towards a foe who throws herself upon their merciful consideration, it still remains a question whether they will do justice to Turkey if they do not insist that she at least shall bo repaid for the enormous outlay she has been obliged to incur, and for the barbarous and treacherous destruction of her fleet at Sinope. It does not meet the j justice of the case to allege that Russia is too impoverished and exhausted by the war to be able to pay an indemnity. We do not believe in the permanent exhaustion of a great nation. It Russia cannot pay now, she may pledge hermay, in commercial phrase, give her bills, not at two or three þÿyears date ; aud Turkey will no doubt be glad to grant her the time and accommodation requisite. Whatever may be thought in Prussia, or even in Austria, of such a proposal, we do not think there are many men in France or England, unless they be Greeks of Manchester or Liverpool, who would think that a hard measure was thus meted out to a gross offender, or that unnecessary or impolitic humiliation was inflicted. Russia would neither be ruined nor very seriously inyield to mere bullying, come whence it may. i' commoded by being compelled to pay to Turkey the sum of ten or twenty millions sterling. At the close of the war in 1815 France was forced to pay upwards of il(50,000,000 as indemnity ; and, moreover, to maintain an army of occupation

of 150,000 men for three years after the peace. And yet France was not ruined by this severity of exaction, but, on the contrary, gained strength from the efforts that were rendered necessary to meet it. And why should a different measure bo dealt out to Russia ? A pecuniary fine of this amount would not only be an act of pure justice to Turkey, but would in all probability tend to the development of the industrial and commercial resources of Russia herself, aud prove to the present and to luturo Czars how much wiser, safer, and more profitable it is to grow wealthy by the sure arts of peace than by insecure conquests or continual warfare and aggression against her neighbours. þÿ =. þÿ

In the Journal des Debats , a few days ago, appeared an article, apparently written on good authority, which throws a light upon the motives which probably influenced Russia in her sudden þÿ þÿacceptance of the Peace proposals of the Allies. According to this statement of the Debats, the French Emperor had communicated to Austria, and through her to other German Powers, his conviction (which other clear-sighted men had not delayed so long to receive) that Russia was more seriously vulnerable on the side of Poland than upon any other ; that by attacking her at her maritime extremities, the Allies were but nibbling at her ; but that if the war continued, they would be compelled, at the risk of all enmities, of all international jealousies or dangers, to strike a more decisive blow, and this could only be dealt across Prussia. In other words, a prolongation of the war must necessarily lead to the traversing of Germany by a French army. Austria, at first deprecating such an extremity, is reported not only at last to have admitted it, but to have consented even to discuss what should be done with Poland, during a tem porary occupation. þÿ Circumstantial þÿdetails, says the Debats, þÿ were entered into, having regard to the restoration of Poland. The victors were to dispose of the Russian provinces. Indemnified by Moldavia and Wallacbia, Austria would give up Galacia to favour and promote the arrangements, and Prussia was to be compelled to abandon þÿPosen. The writer in the Dcbats proceeds to say that

the King of Prussia became suddenly so much alarmed by the gravity of this condition of affairs as to declare that self-preservation must compel him to join the anti-Muscovite alliance. Such, according to the Debats, were the motives that persuaded the Czar to acquiesce at once in the conditions of Austria ; and such the vista of hope opening to the view of the brave and gallant men who now not unnaturally murmur and complain of the peace which so abruptly closes it.
THE PEACE þÿCONGRESS THE VIENNA PROTOCOL. The French and British Ministers at Vienna received instructions on Thursday, the 31st ult., to sign the so-often

\ T, <© ® a 2L AT i 3. mentioned protocol. Immediately after the receipt of the despatches, Sir Hamilton Seymour and M. de Bourqueney communicated their contents to the Austrian Minister for Foreign Affairs and to the Turkish Embassy. In the course of the evening it was settled that the Representatives of England, France, Turkey, and Russia should meet at the Foreign Office at twelve next day, and then and there sign the important document in question. At the appointed hour the four foreign diplomatists had assembled, and they and Count Buol attached their signatures to the subjoined protocol : þÿ In consequence of the acceptance by their respective Courts of the five propositions contained in the the document hereunto annexed, under title of Draught of Preliminaries, the undersigned, after having paraphrased it, conformably to authorisation received to that effect, have agreed that their Governments shall each nominate Plenipotentiaries, who, furnished with the full powers necessary for proceeding to the signature of formal preliminaries of peace, shall conclude an armistice and a definite treaty of peace. The said Plenipotentiaries will have to assemble at Paris within the term of three weeks

be done. Done at Vienna this 1st day of February, 1856. Prince Gortschakoff, when signing the protocol, asked that Prussia might he invited to take part in the Conferences, in which request he was supported by Count Buol. M. de Bourqueney and Sir Hamilton Seymour said they must refer to their Governments on that point.

The names of the negotiators at the approaching Paris Conference are formally given. There are eleven in all. Count Walewski and Baron de Bourqueney represent France ; Lords Clarendon and Cowley, England ; Count de Buol-Schanenstein and Baron de Hubner, Austria; Aali Pacha and Mehemed Djemil Bey, Turkey; the Chevalier þÿd Azeglio, Sardinia; and Count Orloff and Baron Brunnow, Russia. Lord Palmerston has announced that there will be an armistice, but declines to say anything of its terms; though it is to be hoped that a point very properly raised by Sir l)e Lacy Evans þÿ namely, whether Russia is to use the sea, during the armistice, for fetching and carrying soldiers and stores þÿ has not escaped attention. It is rumoured that the period will reach to the 3lsl March. By that time the ice in the Baltic will not be a þÿ material þÿguarantee for the safety of Russia, so, that if the negotiations should be juggled into a sham, our fleet may yet distinguish itself. The Sebastopol docks are, it is stated, now utterly destroyed; so, with the ships at the bottom of the sea, and the means of reproducing them taken aivav, the limitation of the Russian fleet is temporarily complete. Such a humiliation has never been inflicted since gun powder was invented. It can never be forgiven, and the certainty that it will not should make the Allies doubly careful to þÿ take such þÿorder that the revenge of the chastised enemy may never be formidable.
FRANCE. So far have the expectations relative to the conclusion of peace been carried that the names of some of the Sovereigns of Europe are already cited as about to visit Paris on the signature of

the treaty. Among these figures that of the Emperor Alexander. There seems a certain probability that the Emperor of Austria will fulfil this rumour; his conduct during the progress of the arrangements with Russia having strongly cemented the friendship and confidence existing between him and the Emporor of the French.

Enlistment of a Woman in the 97th Regiment, at Windsor. þÿ A smart and rather interesting young person from the Emerald Isle, only seventeen, and upwards of five feet seven inches in height, enlisted yesterday week into the 17th, a recruiting party of that regiment being quartered at Windsor. The young recruit slept that evening where they were several beds occupied by men, and on the following morning was marched, with other recruits, to the hospital, to undergo the customary examination by the doctor. After partly undressing the recruit was told to strip, when the saidisant soldier said, þÿ I find I can no longer disguise my sex; I am a woman; hut if I cannot be enlisted as a soldier I will be a sailor, as I am determined to go to the þÿEast. The poor young girl was ultimately taken by a corporal of the guard before the borough magis trates, charged with obtaining the þÿQueen smoney under false pretences, hut this she ingeniously refuted by saying, þÿ I simply answered þÿ -Yes, to the enlisting sergeant, who, when he gave me the shilling, asked if I was able and willing to serve the Queen: and so L am at this moment both able and willing to do þÿso. She was ultimately remanded for a few days, and in the meantime the magistrates will determine what can be done for her. In the sequel, it appeared that the girl has got a sweetheart in the 4th Dragoon Guards, who is now with his regiment in the Crimea, and being determined, under every hazard and difficulty, to follow her lover, eiw

listed into the 97th, upon hearing that the regiment was going out to the East in the course of a few weeks. The townspeople as well as the military, sympathising with the young girl, have already commenced a subscription for her, and the soldiers are very zealous in sending from their mess the best it will afford, during her temporary incarceration. It has since been ascertained that she came to Windsor from Brighton, where her mother at present resides 'I'lie girl enlisted in the name of Thomas Wood, but this has been ascertained to be a fictitious one.

DEMERARA. þÿr row //rt Royal Gazette, Feb. 23.) We regret to say that serious disturbances have taken place during the past week throughout the colony : and the shops of the Portuguese traders have been pillaged and destroyed by the negro population. There lias been for a long time existing among the Creole negroes a latent feeling against the Portuguese immigrants, who are a thrifty and industrious race of people, and this feeling is also prevalent among the African immigrants and negroes from the islands who have come to reside here. This latent feeling of jealousy would not have broken out into active hostility but for other circumstances which have occurred in this city within the last few weeks. About the end of the past year, a man named John Sayers Orr better known in England and in America by the cognomen of the þÿ Angel Gabriel, þÿ or as the people of Scotland þÿtermed þÿ Wicked þÿKnavish, returned to this Colony, of which he is a creole, and took up his abode with his mother in this city. This man, who is a sort of religious fanatic, having created serious riots attended with bloodshed in New Yoik, Montreal, Greenock and Glasgow, by the violence of his language, had not been many days in this Colony before he commenced his old trade of disturbing the public peace by violent harrangucs against the Homan Catholics whom he accused of all sorts of crimes and immoralities. Had he confined himself to this kind of preaching he might have preached till dooms-day be-

fore he would have succeeded in influencing the minds, or arousing the passions of the ignorant portion of the black population ; but having discovered that there was a considerable degree of smothered jealousy and ill-feeling existing between the negro population and the Portuguese, he adroitly seized upon that and mixed it up with his attacks on the Koman Catholics In this he was only too successful þÿ like a spark dropped upon tinder, hostility against thp Portuguese spread rapidly throughout the city, and was soon communicated to the country districts. In Georgetown the Portuguese where assailed by men women and children, the cries of þÿ Down with the Portuguese, Down with the Pope þÿ! summoued by the Governor on Monday the 18th The Portuguese exhibited very considerable forbearance þÿ and however much they may have been annoyed, they did not commit any breach of the peace in resenting the insults offered to them. Thus matters went on until Sunday the I Oth inst., when Orr mounted the town pump, in front of Stabrock Market, armed with a dagger and life-preserver and addressed a large crowd of persons in a most inflammatory manner. For the seditious language used by him on that occasion, and for convening an unlawful assembly, he has since been arrested and committed to take his trial before the Supreme Criminal Court in April next. Hut we are anticipating events. In consequence of the inflammatory and seditious language used by Orr in his addresses, and also of the evident ill-feeling which he had exci-

ted amongst the Negroes against the Portuguese the Governor on the 1 oth inst., issued a proclamation forbidding unlawful assemblages of people on the streets. On the 17th Orr was prevented from preaching in the streets þÿ and be then proceeded to his þÿmother s yard and there he addressed the crowd who assembled to hear him' After this meeting, on Sunday evening, the disturbances commenced by the negroes attacking one or two Portuguese shops and pelting several Portuguese, who had assembled in the neighbourhood. I his row was suppressed by the Police, and the night passed off without further disturbance

z X 8 i'DU A T i 3, On Monday morning Feb. 18, the disturbances re-commenced. þÿOrr sexamination before the Police Magistrate was appointed to take place at twelve þÿo clock, but long before that hour, a large crowd assembled on the Brick-dam on which the Head Police Station and the Police þÿMagistrate s office are situated. Between 10 and 11 þÿo clock the crowd became excited, and a Portuguese was pursued on the charge of having stabbed a creole. The man was immediately apprehended by the Police, but not before he had sustained personal injury. The Police turned out in force under the command of Inspector Horne. The Horse Police speedily dispersed the mob þÿ and the examination of Mr. Orr was conducted and concluded with perfect tranquility. The people however, almost immediately commenced their attacks upon the Portuguese shops in the outlyiug parts of the town, and by midnight there was not one in those districts which had not been completely gutted of its contents. A large body of special constables had been sworn in to aid the police. Between seven and eight þÿo clock a formidable riot occurred in the Charlestown district, and the Military were called out. A guard of the 2d West India Regiment, consisting of 2 sergeants corporals, drummer, 2 1 and 40 men, were sent to the þÿ1 olice-stationunder the command of Lieut. þÿBrewit and another of 1 Serjeant and 20 men was stationed at the gaol where Mr. Orr who had been unable to find bail, was confined. These guards have been continued
